subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 1, consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to congratulate heartily the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon both his arrangement and his presentation of the budget on Friday last. In my opinion it was highly creditable alike to the minister and to the officials of the Department of Finance, and I am bound to say, if he will permit me, that he read a very long document with very great distinctness so that everyone in the house could hear what he was saying.
I should like also to congratulate him upon having delivered a budget speech. For the first time in recent years at least, we have had a budget delivered by a member of the Liberal party; for his predecessor in office prior to May, 1930, did not deliver a budget for the succeeding year, and the now Minister of Finance in May, 1930, merely reviewed the expenditures for the year that had ended on March 31, 1930, and indicated the revenues as they were then known, but made no forecast as to the probable expenditures during the year which was to close on March 31, 1931. Neither did he make any estimate of the

The Budget-Mr. Bennett

probable revenues. I pointed out frequently in years prior to that, that such a course could not by any stretch of the imagination be described as constituting a budget statement. It is therefore a matter of great satisfaction to have before us now a statement that is a budget for the year ending March 31, 1937. The minister has indicated the probable revenues of the country and the sources from which they will be derived, and also the probable expenditures and the channels through which they will be made.
I should like, however, to direct attention to the fact that speaking on May 1, 1930, the then Minister of Finance apparently had no appreciation of the great world forces that were marching toward a world depression. He apparently had entirely overlooked the fact that we were on the edge of, in fact had already entered into, that depression period. The government of that day seemed to have had exactly the same view; for I recall that the then Prime Minister, speaking only in April of that year, said:
The fact that hon. members are obliged to restrict themselves to naming individual municipalities and are able to name them in numbers that can be counted on one hand so far as the Dominion of Canada is concerned, demonstrates more strongly than words could how little we have a national problem of unemployment in this country at the jjresent time.
That was in April, 1930. When in 1928 and 1929 attention was directed from this side of the house to world movements which, in our judgment at least, meant inevitable disaster to the prosperity which then was abroad and to the movements in the stock exchanges, we were regarded as pessimists, and we find that as late as May 1, 1930, the Minister of Finance said:
Before touching on the dominion's finances for the fiscal year just ended may I survey a few of the events which have indirectly influenced the balance sheet. As we all know, national revenues are dependent on the volume of business transacted. During the year certain unusual factors made themselves felt, in particular, the delayed marketing of the grain crops and the great decline in prices of stocks in the latter months of the year. While these factors are important they cannot be considered as permanently prejudicial to our economic structure.
Further in his opening observations, having referred to the fact that our harvest had not yet been moved and that it was very remarkable that in the preceding year harvester excursions had not been run to provide the west with harvest help, and having referred also to the condition of industry, he said:
We have marshalled our resources to meet the problems arising from delayed marketing of the grain crops and, at the same time,
[Mr. Bennett. [
absorbed the shock resulting from tens of millions of dollars being suddenly withdrawn from the ordinary reservoirs of credit.
I point that out for this reason: that as the Minister of Finance was in May, 1930, wholly unable to appreciate conditions that indicated a world catastrophe, so I venture to think that on Friday last he somewhat overestimated the forces making towards world recovery. I do that because I regard it as somewhat important that we should have no misunderstanding as to the extent to which the forces of recovery have operated in the world at large and in our own country in particular. Within three months of the date of the making of that statement by the Minister of Finance it was apparent that the views that were held by those who then sat to the left of the Speaker were sound; for our customs duties for April, May, June and July in the year 1930-31 as compared with the year 1929-30 had fallen by 815,815,000, excise taxes by $5,800,000, and excise duties by $547,000, being a net decrease in revenue during that short period of over $22,000,000. I think it is equally true that the income tax collections were somewhat larger than in the previous year, because they were collected on the incomes of 1929. But. the absolute, shall I say, disregard and overlooking of these conditions constituted in my opinion a grave error in judgment on the part of the minister.
There has been much misunderstanding about the many things that have happened during the last five years and I am going to refer shortly to some of the events that have brought about the conditions to which the hon. gentleman) referred. If I took up a much longer time I could not more clearly indicate the progress of this country during the last year or two than to use the words of the Minister of Finance. I am sure there is not an hon. member of this bouse who will say for a single minute that any policies of the present government had anything to do with the condition of affairs in Canada on December 31, 1935. Those conditions, whether good or bad, whether evil or otherwise, were brought about because of the policies pursued by the previous government from August, 1930, up to the end of October, 1935. As there was no opportunity for parliament to meet between October and December, it is obvious that the great improvement to which the bon. gentleman has referred and the figures which he has given are a complete vindication of the policies pursued by the government of that day during the last few years. Perhaps this could not be summed up better than it was in a single

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
paragraph in the speech of the minister. I quote from page 2367 of Hansard, as follows:
I am pleased to be able to report, for the fiscal year just ended, an important gain in our total trade with other countries, amounting in round figures to 152 million dollars. This is an increase of 12-8 per cent over the previous year. It is true that world trade generally has improved during the past year, but it should l)e noted that while the average increase in trade of 24 leading countries in the calendar year 1935 was 4-1 per cent our own trade increase was 11-3 per cent. As a result of this marked expansion in our foreign commerce Canada has moved up from eighth to sixth place among the nations in total world trade.
In that paragraph is contained a complete vindication of what, during all those long years, those who now sit opposite to me denounced in season and out of season with a heartlessness which at times I think aroused the animosity of some Canadians. They pursued their guerrilla warfare and, as I say, constantly in season and out of season denounced the policies that I have lived long enough to see a minister of finance of a new government stand in his place and say have brought to this country that regeneration for which we are looking and that improvement for which we are striving. Hon. gentlemen smile; they may smile but they cannot change the record as it was made by the minister. When the other twenty-four great trading nations of the world showed an improvement of only a little over four per cent, the improvement in our country was more than eleven per cent. Under these circumstances should we not as Canadians be proud that those who toiled, though they did not have the same political faith and opinions as the government of to-day, by " their efforts and through the policies which they formulated, have been able to accomplish the ends for which the minister now takes credit?
If recovery has commenced, it is a recovery based upon policies that this government did not initiate or control. That, I think, will have to 'be admitted. If that recovery is greater than it has been in the other twenty-four great trading countries of the world, three times as great, then there must be some credit given to those who initiated the policies that brought about that result in. Canada. When the Liberal government resigned in 1930, this is the legacy they left us: First of all, commitments had been made for millions of dollars, many having been initiated and created under orders in council passed between the date of the defeat of the government and their resignation. Second, a treaty with New Zealand terminated on that
12739-160}
very day. Third, a shrinkage in trade that amounted to over twenty per cent of the trade of the preceding year, as well as a shrinkage in revenue of a like per cent. Fourth, our railway revenue had diminished to such an extent that immediate steps were necessary to provide funds for the enterprise. Fifth, the reports made to the bureau of statistics showed that at that time unemployment was shown to the extent of 113.000, by reporting companies or enterprises which constitute about half of all those engaged in industry in Canada.

I think I said that very clearly. We found the stock exchanges in the condition to which the minister referred. On May 1, 1930, we found the provinces practically unable to pay their obligations and looking for means for that purpose. I shall not go into the matter at greater length, although I could if I so desired.
During the ensuing five years, what has been the result? One hon. gentleman opposite referred the other day to the fact that trade through his port had fallen off by more than one-half what it was in 1930. I think it is very desirable that our relations with the other countries of the world should be clearly understood. The other day the Minister of Finance stated something that people sometimes forget when he said that we in Canada are powerless to remove the uncertainties in the world s political outlook. So in this country with eleven million people we have to compare our position with that of the other countries of the world. I think it is very important that we should have a clear understanding of just what has been our position with relation to the other countries of the world since 1929. Let me point out, first, that according to The League of Nations reports, during the great depression world trade fell to 31 [DOT] 3 per cent of what it was in 1929. Some put the figures at just exactly one-third of what it was, but the figures collected by the League of Nations show the figure as 34-3 per cent. This represents the extent to which world trade had decreased.

speechtext:
Yes, but in similar terms. What the League of Nations collected was comparisons of comparable things reduced to a common denominator. Let us look at 1929 to see what Canada was doing. That was one of our great years. In that year our export trade was 3-71 per cent of the world's total export trade. That is not imports, but exports-I want to make that clear. In 1929, 3-71 per cent of the world's export trade was done by the Dominion of Canada. In the calendar year 1930 we did 3-42 per cent of the world's export trade. In 1931 it had fallen to 3-29 per cent, and in 1932 it was 3-78, there being an increase over the preceding year. In 1933 it was 3-59 per cent, in 1934, 3-99 per cent, and last year, the calendar year 1935, the League of Nations reports that the export trade of the Dominion of Canada had risen to 4-32 per cent of the world's export trade. That, it will be observed, is a considerably larger percentage of the world's export trade than we did in the year 1929. Our proportion of imports however, for reasons to which presently I will direct attention, was much less because we were steadily diminishing our import trade. The reasons for that were I think apparent to every thoughtful Canadian. In the calendar year 1929 we did 3-65 per cent of the world's import t-rade; in 1930, 3'47; in 1931, 2-91; in 1932, 2-75; in 1933, 2-28; in 1934, 2-60; and in 1935 we did 2-71 per cent of the world's import trade.
Now take the two, add your imports and exports together and ascertain what percentage of the world's trade was done by the Dominion of Canada during the dark five years from 1930 to 1935. In 1929 we did 3-68 per cent of the world's entire trade; in 1930, 3-45 per cent; in 1931, 3-09; in 1932, 3-24; in 1933, 2'94; in 1934, 3-27; and in 1935 we did 3-49 per cent of the entire trade of the world. I give these figures because they bear closely upon the statement made by the minister himself and which I have just read. Then there was another significant fact, one to which the minister referred the other day, and I think very properly, namely, that during the last few years we have modified to a great extent the visible commodity trading balances -of the country; and by reason of gold being (exported as a commodity we had been able to create a very large favourable balance.
The minister referred the other day to our tourist trade, but I leave that entirely out of the matter for the reason that you have to consider other factors as well as the tourist trade. There are insurance premiums; there

is interest that has to be paid abroad and there is interest from abroad; and there are other items that go into the invisibles that make up the ultimate balance of trade. Sc that I will leave out the tourist trade for the moment and confine myself entirely, exclusive of gold, to our commodity balance.
Our commodity balances when we came into office were running steadily against us. In 1930 I could not understand the government of the day reducing the sales tax by half, as they pointed out, and taking other action that was suggested to be a lessening of the burden of taxation at a time when we were urgently in need of revenues; and the shrinkage in these revenues was apparent during the operations of the month of April itself. Now without going into it at length, let me say that in 1921 we had a favourable balance of $17,000,000; in 1928 we had a favourable balance of $151,000,000; but in
1929	we had an unfavourable commodity balance of $103,000,000, and in 1931 of $10,000,000, because the corrective measures that were put in operation in the fall of
1930	had not immediately become apparent. So that in 1932 we had a favourable balance of $49,000,000; in 1933, $136,000,000; in 1934, $146,000,000, and last year, $192,000,000, exclusive of gold, which we will treat as a commodity and which brings about the situation to which the minister referred.
The other day it was pointed out, not improperly, that too much importance may at times be attached to what is called the balance of trade; but there is no possible likelihood of anyone ever gainsaying what was said by the minister the other day as to the importance of the balance of trade when you come to consider its effect upon the stabilizing . of the value of your unit, your dollar abroad among the selling and purchasing countries of the world. It was that factor which we had to consider when we dealt with the matter in 1930. These significant facts indicate, I think, just what we had to face when we came to assume the responsibilities of government in 1930. But there are two or three other matters that might be mentioned when dealing with trade.
In 1935 we increased our domestic exports over 1932 by 47-7 per cent; over 1933 by 37-2 per cent and over 1934 by 11-6, showing that we had made steady progress during those years. Now we come to what I regard as one of the most important matters with which we had to deal, namely, the steps to be taken to correct the conditions to which I have referred. What steps would be suggested? First of all, as has been pointed out in this house very frequently, we raised the tariffs. We certainly

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
did. We raised tariffs in the fall of 1930 at the special session for a very deliberate and definite purpose. We were confronted with a situation such as this country had never faced before, and it became absolutely essential for us to take some steps to safeguard the integrity of the nation.
Now raising tariffs does not necessarily mean increased costs to the consumers. I realized then as I do now the difficulties that have always to be met when tariffs are raised, because it is contended that there is an increased price to the consumer; and so we had regard to the fact that there was, as is pointed out in one of the reports of the tariff board to which I may refer before I conclude, a chaotic condition in many industries in the United States which were seeking, under the lower tariffs that prevailed between Canada and the United States, to find here a market for their surplus products. And they were finding that market. If you take the trade figures you will realize that they were finding that market in increased volume; and every time a dollar's worth of goods came in from that country, industrially chaotic at the time, it displaced a dollar's worth of Canadian industrial effort and deprived the Canadian of his work, throwing him into the ranks of the unemployed.
Faced with that situation we determined that the proper course to pursue was to enact tariff leigislation that would give Canadians an equal opportunity with those who competed with them in their own markets; secondly, legislation that would ensure employment of Canadians to supply the wants of Canadians; and thirdly, we had to take such steps as might be necessary to ensure the consumer against exploitation. How did we do it? If hon. gentlemen will take the trouble to turn to Hansard of May 13, 1930, they will find there a list of communications signed by various industrial firms in Canada, by which they undertook that they would not raise prices to the consumer in Canada if they w'ere afforded an opportunity to secure the Canadian market for their own products. That was in 1930, in the fall.

There is the interpretation of the figures as given by the minister himself, and when I point out that since 1932 there has been not only a steady increase in imports and exports with the United Kingdom but also a steady increase in our trade with the British empire as a whole, I only indicate the importance of that trade as it has been indicated by the language of the minister. These words I commend to the house:
Over fifty-six per cent of our imports come from the United States. At the same time they take only thirty-seven per cent of our exports. From empire countries we purchase about one-third of our imports and sell to them just over one-half our goods exported.

What is more, every fair-minded man admits it. I have not seen any man who has really taken the figures and analyzed them who would not say that this was the result of those agreements between the Dominion of Canada, the motherland and the British empire. But for some strange reason men think it improper to admit a fact. Politics produces strange effects upon given people.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, hon. gentlemen
may say "hear, hear," but the truth of the matter is indicated by the records. You may take the imports and exports of this country with the British empire in 1931, in 1932 and in succeeding years, and I say that no reasonably fair-minded Canadian reading that record will deny that the agreements then entered into brought about the conditions to which the hon. gentleman referred in his speech the other day. That being so, Mr. Speaker, recall the language that was used in those days: "A Tory conspiracy." Those were the words that were quoted with respect to the men who gathered here from every part of the far-flung empire to make agreements that have had the effect these agreements have had: over one-half our exports have gone to empire countries. Look at our trade with Australia and South Africa; look at the increased trade under the treaty we made with New Zealand. We had to make a new treaty with New Zealand, and that treaty has brought about increased trade and has added wealth to both countries. Take Australia or South Africa or Great Britain; analyze our trade with any one of them, and you will find exactly the same trend. I was glad to hear the minister indicate the other day what the trend was.
I am going to put it this way now: If hon. gentlemen opposite attach no importance to these agreements and loudly cheer the sentiment that they have no value to Canada; if they are of no value, as the hon. gentleman says, I venture to suggest that he will not find much difficulty in discovering other countries who would be willing to take over these agreements, if they could have them. More than that, he will find it somewhat difficult to convince many people that these agreements have no appreciable value, and especially will that be so when he is confronted with the necessity of renewing them in 1937. That is the position he will have to face then. Of course it will be very simple at that time to say, "Well, we are not particular about that; there is no value to us in these agreements. You can have this, that and the other thing; they are of no value to us." That is the atttitude that has been taken

by hon. gentlemen opposite this afternoon, and of course that will make it very simple to deal with those with whom you must negotiate next year.
Then there arises another point, and I might as well deal with it now. The other afternoon the hon. gentleman referred to the fact that in the budget there had been a great extension of free entry to British goods coming into Canada. I wondered if he had been reading what had taken place since 1932. When we made the agreements in that year, this country was at the lowest level of its economic life. We had to face a situation in which we could not, for the reasons I have already given with respect to trade and finance, throw down our tariff barriers, if you call them such, and permit free trade, or, shall I say, a very low tariff trade, to come into this country. We told our friends in Great Britain what our position was, and I think you will find that since 1932 we have steadily, although slowly, enlarged their market jn this country. If the hon. member will look at the budget delivered last year by the Minister of Finance he will find that the number of items affecting goods from Great Britain that we placed on the free list amount altogether to over 250. He will find that between 1932 and 1935 there had been an increase of the original number by something like 100. There had also been a removal of the excise tax of three per cent, one and a half per cent in one year and one and a half per cent the next year, and a diminution or lessening of specific duties in other cases. So we had widened and broadened opportunities for British products in our own market. We had done that, explaining to them that we could not maintain the integrity of Canada if we were to permit duties to be so low as to lead to the destruction of our industrial structure, and throw out of employment large numbers of people.
A treaty with New Zealand; a treaty with France-what did we do with respect to France? We gave notice to terminate the treaty then existing with France. We were told at the time that it was a terrible thing for a young country of eleven million people to dare to terminate a treaty with an old and populous country such as France. Nevertheless we terminated that treaty. Why? All you have to do is to look at that treaty, and you will realize the reason why. Then we negotiated a new treaty. My friend the then Secretary of State spent many weeks in France, and in 1934 we made a supplementary treaty. The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) referred to the fact that the extensions that were referred to

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
by the Minister of Finance were arranged by the preceding government, not by the present administration at all.
So much for the treaty with France. Then we made a treaty with Germany by which we gave Germany the intermediate tariff, a procedure which was much approved at that time, because it was said it gave a wider opportunity to us to sell goods in Germany by reason of securing the minimum tariff. In some of the tariff items about to be considered by this house and the committee of the whole it will be found that the extension of the favoured nation treatment to the United States involves also an extension to all countries enjoying favoured nation treatment from Canada. We extended the intermediate tariff to Austria, and made a trade agreement with them. It was largely negotiated in London by the then Secretary of State. We made a treaty with Brazil and we made a treaty with Poland. Notwithstanding the conditions under which we lived, depressed conditions and a shrinkage of trade throughout the world, we were able to make treaties of commerce and trade with the countries to which I have referred, thereby extending the market for our exports on terms and conditions which I have already indicated. That in itself, if hon. members opposite had done it, would have been heralded from the housetops as a wondrous achievement. The fact that the other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce made slight reference to a few items in the French treaty, which were arranged by his predecessor. necessitated the Minister of Finance making special reference to it in his budget. The reference is in this budget.
Then, let us go a step farther. How long had we been endeavouring to extend our trade with Germany? The former minister of finance, of the Liberal party, had been endeavouring unsuccessfully to make arrangements, but we did succeed in making an agreement with them by which we gave them the intermediate tariff in exchange for their minimum tariff. That applies to Austria. With some slight modifications it is true with respect to Poland.
And what about the new treaty with France? In this connection I shall quote an independent authority. I do not know how accurate his view may be, but he says that "it is the most workable and fair-minded treaty that hasjever been made between France and Canada." We have had a treaty ever since very early days. There has been a general recognition by each of the position of the other. We arrived at arrangements which I believe were fair and equitable to both, and they were not difficult to arrange. From time to time they have purchased large quantities of our wheat,
although our export figures did not show anything like the amount indicated by their import figures, due to the shifting of the ports to which wheat is delivered. One year since 1930 they took from us 36,000.000 bushels of wheat, and they made it abundantly clear to us that they were prepared to take all available wheat that they might require so long as they could secure in Canada a fair market for certain of their products, notably wines and champagnes. We introduced into that particular treaty a provision which stated that the treatment received by us with respect to our wheat production should be in the very same spirit as that accorded to France with respect to the products of her vineyards. We carried that into effect. I mention this because in the light of what has transpired it becomes important to realize that during all the depression period, with all the attacks that were levelled against the administration of the day, there was a gradual and continued expansion of our markets; greater opportunity was afforded to sell our wheat abroad. We could not have maintained the integrity of our economic life had we not taken such action, and the concessions offered in our markets were made coextensive with the possibility of maintenance of our own economic structure. Wherever we could we granted concessions to those who had been granting concessions to us.
Some reference was made to the relations of this country with Japan. I shall not do more than say that the matter has been discussed at some length in the house. It remained for a Canadian government to provide by legislation that when a nation complains of a value fixed by the Canadian minister and an appeal is taken to the tariff board, which is constituted as a court, and the appeal is not prosecuted or terminated within a certain time, Canada is non-suited and the appellant is restored to his original position without further question. That applies to all nations, not only to Japan. When I make that statement, of course, I refer to all nations receiving favoured nation treatment from Canada. So that so far as we are concerned we have afforded opportunity for appeal and then provided that if the appeal so taken is not disposed of within a given time we must lose the appeal, so far as Canada is concerned. The minister is overruled by the other country, whatever that country may be, and is held up to ridicule for having placed upon a commodity a wholly erroneous value for duty purposes. That is the first time I have ever known of the introduction of such a principle into the fiscal or judicial life of a country.
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

Let me deal now with the problem connected with the exemption to the extent of $100 on goods coming from the United States. Perhaps this is the better time to deal with the matter, although a discussion on it might be more logical a little later. The minister will recall that he referred to the treaty made between Canada and the United States. I observe already the shrinkage in customs revenues resulting from that treaty, a shrinkage which will result from it to a greater and greater extent. There has not been a minister of finance in Canada in the last forty years who has not desired to make such an arrangement, but those ministers knew they dare not do it without at the same time endangering their country's integrity. Why? This agreement made with the United States extends to every country to which we give favoured nation treatment. Travellers who cross the sea may all bring in, if they so desire, one hundred dollars' worth of commodities if they have been forty-eight hours in a foreign country, and they can do that three times a year. I wonder if it is known just how many travellers, for instance, went from our ocean ports last year. From ocean ports there left this country last year, apparently as travellers and tourists, some 28,152 people, without including those who went from the Pacific. So it is not too much to say that by water we have about 30,000 people leaving our ocean ports. But when we come to the United States of America and ask how many automobiles and how many passengers entered that country from Canada, I fancy that a great many of our friends will be as greatly surprised as I was, for according to the figures given by the United States authorities, 2,135,999 persons entered the United States from Canada in the year 1935 by automobile, and by rail and steamer another 366,288, making a total of 2,502,287, and if you include the 30,000 odd that I have mentioned you have a grand total of 2.532.287. I desire to point out that these people did not all have their own automobile, but the average was three people per automobile, or slightly over that, and the number of automobiles that entered the United States from Canada was 659,259.
Now, I put this to you, and it is a fair question: Can this country stand the entrance into its markets free of duty of twenty dollars' worth per head of commodities for two and a half million people? To the extent that goods are acquired from foreign countries under the provisions of that arrangement, whether it be from Great Britain or France of Belgium or Spain or the United States, we have made Canada a free trade area within

their country. I say this, sir, that previous ministers of finance felt that they dare not- and I use that word advisedly, because I have discussed it with many of them-take the risk that is involved in a country with only eleven millions of people giving free entry to the extent of possibly $300 a year per head of those who come back to this country after forty-eight hours stay in France or Spain or the United States. I take that figure of two and a half millions of people, and at $20 per head it means fifty million dollars; at $40 per head it means one hundred million dollars; and when you remember the figures I gave as to the volume of our trade with the United States then indeed the members of this house may well ask themselves whether we can afford that luxury or not.
Would I like to see it done? Yes, sir. Would I like to see it carried into effect? Yes, sir. Would every Canadian who goes to and from and trades and barters like to see it done? I think the answer is yes, but there are many things that this country must now learn it cannot do that it would like to do. We would like to have built three railroads across the country, and we did so, but we now know that we should never have done it. I could mention other matters of the same kind, and I mention this because it seems to me it is just as well to mention it here as anywhere else, and dispose of that once and for all.
Now I will deal with our financial position. Shortly after the late government came into office it examined our financial position, and on the first of October we had to go to the market of New York and borrow $100,000,000 at four per cent. We were confronted with the necessity of finding money for the railroad with maturing obligations, and after consulting with the best financial minds it was determined that that was the moment, then or never, having regard to what was happening in the world at large, to raise this money, and so we raised it in the United States at that time. That $100,000,000 is still a liability in the United States of America, being practically all held there. That was our first venture into the market of the United States to secure money to meet our situation at home.
But in 1931 we realized that this country could not continue if it did not make some effort to lessen the burden of debt service, and so we asked the people of Canada to convert their high interest bearing securities to a lower rate. I recall the circumstances very well. It was said that it would be hopeless to undertake to do such a thing at that

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
time, and yet the government of the day believed that the Canadian people would respond. The result was that nearly 8650,000,000 of these securities were converted, effecting a saving larger than any other that was made, a saving in interest of over $6,250,000 per annum. As a result of that conversion and of the sale of treasury bills, to which I shall presently refer, brought about through the creation and organization of a central bank, the Bank of Canada, we were able to reduce before we left office the annual interest charge upon this country by approximately $16,000,000. When I heard my friend the Minister of Finance the other day refer to the saving of interest I thought he might at least have pointed out that $16,000,000 of that saving had been effected by his predecessors in office, that $16,000,000 of that saving in interest charges had been brought about by the conversions to which I have referred.

Side by side with .that, was the great drive the government made to secure lower rates of interest. Does anyone think that these lower rates of interest came about by accident? Does he think for a single moment there was no conscious action on the part of any government or organization to bring about that end? First of all. it was necessary to secure a lowering of the rate of interest for deposits in the banks. The provincial authorities had to be considered, hecause in some places they were maintaining savings institutions and paying a higher rate of interest. There were also the building and loan organizations and trust companies to be considered. First, there was the securing of a lesser rate on deposits and then the making of a lower market. In that regard it wild be recalled that when the imperial conference met here in 1932 we adopted a resolution which had for its purpose that very end. It will be recalled that one of the resolutions we adopted was in these terms:
As regards monetary factors, the conference recognizes that the central position of the United Kingdom, not only among the countries of the commonwealth but in world trade and finance, makes the United Kingdom a main factor in anything that can be done. The conference therefore welcomes the following statement made on behalf of the United Kingdom by the Chancellor of the Exchequer:
"His Majesty's government desire to see wholesale sterling prices rise. The best condition for this would be a rise in gold prices and the absence of a rise in gold prices inevitably imposes limitations on what can be done for sterling. A rise in prices cannot be effected by monetary action alone, since various other factors which have combined to bring about the present depression must also be modified or removed before a remedy is assured. His Majesty's government nevertheless recognize that an ample supply of shortterm money at low rates may have a valuable influence, and they are confident that the efforts which have successfully brought about the present favourable monetary conditions can and will, unless unforeseen difficulties arise, be continued."
(d) The conference recommends the other countries of the commonwealth represented here to act in conformity with the line of policy as set out in the statement of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, so far as lies within their power.
In the monetary sphere the primary line of action towards a rise in prices should be the creation and maintenance, within the limits of sound finance, of such conditions as

will assist in the revival of enterprise and trade. Among these conditions are low rates of interest and an abundance of short-term money.	While regard must	be	had	to thedifferent conditions applying to various types of loans, the rate of interest for all purposes should be kept as low as financial conditions permit.	At	the same time	it	is necessary
that these favourable monetary conditions be achieved, not by the inflationary creation of additional means of payment to finance public expenditure, but by an orderly monetary policy, safeguarded if the necessity should arise, by such steps as will restrain and circumscribe the scope of violent speculative movements in commodities or securities.
Upon that policy His Majesty's government	in	Canada acted.	At the	worldeconomic	conference	in	1933	it waspointed	out	that twenty-five	cent	metal
coverage was ample for most purposes. In June, 1934, we amended the Dominion Notes Act to provide that up to $120,000,000, a coverage of twenty-five per cent in gold was all that was required, and that silver might be bought to the extent of 1,671,802 fine ounces of newly-mined Canadian silver in each of the calendar years 1934, 1935, 1936 and 1937, which silver shall be purchased and held by the minister pursuant to the section. Then on July 5, 1935, there was enacted a provision for the revaluation of the gold held by the Bank of Canada under the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act, and, further, that there should be established, if it was thought desirable, a stabilization exchange fund. That fund has not been set up because we thought it desirable at that time not to make it imperative upon the Bank of Canada to take that action, but rather to provide that it could be set up, if it was thought desirable, by proclamation, bringing into force the provisions of that statute. As I understand it, at the present moment the provisions of that statute in connection with the exchange fund have not been brought into force.

That has nothing to do with it. The result of all this was to secure a much lower rate of interest, such a rate of interest as we have never had before in this country, a rate which was undreamed of a few years ago and one that was thought almost impossible of achievement.
In this regard I think this is possibly the best place to discuss the situation that has developed in Australia. Sometimes our friends point to Australia as an example that could readily be followed here. Those who are interested will find that in January, 1931, the average yield basis of Commonwealth of Australia domestic issues was about 7i per cent for a government borrower, a very high

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
rate. In November, 1935, an internal issue of 3J's, due in 1949, was placed at 99-75, a yield basis of just over 3-75 per cent. In that same month an issue of the Dominion of Canada 3's, due in 1955, sold readily in our own market at 98-75, to yield 3-08 per cent. Turning to the London market we find Australian 3|'s, due in 1948, selling at around 99, while Canada 3J's, due in 1955, were selling at 102. On the New York stock exchange we find Australian 5's, due in 1955, at 105, as against a quotation of 112 for Canadian 5's, due in 1952. An economist connected -with a Canadian financial house has asked whether one might be pardoned for wondering if Canada's credit, both in domestic and external markets, is not perhaps overrated. Later figures show that our credit is even better than it was according to what I read a moment ago. That is the achievement of the last few- years.
I might point out further that we provided for farm loans at a lower rate of interest, for debt adjustment, as is known, and for loans to provinces, with respect to which I shall have something to say at this moment. The minister the other afternoon pointed out that the government of the day had made loans to provinces. That is absolutely correct; we did make loans to provinces. I am not satisfied that in all cases the provinces have responded as they should with the most careful economy in the expenditure of the moneys thus loaned. In fact the evidence which I have is very clear that such has not always been the case. Nevertheless we were confronted with this , emergency:	Should we
permit the provinces to default or should we endeavour to save them until such time as recovery would warrant our taking the view that if they did default they -would do no great injury to the credit of the Dominion of Canada? As the minister fairly said, wisely or unwisely, we took the step we did; we did provide these provinces with money with which to meet maturing obligations in New York and London, money with which to carry on relief works and for relief purposes, and in some cases, as was pointed out the other day, for part of the work of government itself. But I ask you, Mr. Speaker, I ask my fellow members of this house, whether in the days of the darkest depression, when every part of the .world where money was available was watching and waiting to see whether or not this or that security would fall, we dared take the risk of permitting default on the part of any of the western provinces. I think not; I still think that that was sound. At times I have had grave doubts sis to whether it was wise to continue it beyond a certain point; but
certainly at the time we first did it, had we not done so, I am satisfied that the gravest disaster possible would have overtaken Canada. At least this was the advice I received from those who were informed and were well able to speak with authority. And the government of the day, realizing that they might be subject to severe criticism both in their own country and in other places, felt nevertheless a compelling sense of duty that necessitated their coming to the rescue of these provinces.
May I point out here that in my opinion it was a great mistake for the minister to suggest that he had arrived at some modified scheme in connection with loan councils and national loans. I say that for this reason. Did Alberta have a fair chance? The correspondence was tabled here. Alberta declined. But Alberta did not have what has now been suggested, a modified scheme; Alberta did not have that scheme before it at the time default came about.

Now I come to the question as to the creation of national councils and loan councils. I ventured the belief, rightly or wrongly, wisely or unwisely, that until such time as there were evident signs of recovery there could be no real conversion of the securities of the provinces, the municipalities and the railways. That is to say, we might do it spasmodically; we might deal with some millions in connection with the railways, and we might save two or three millions per annum, as we have; but if we are to do it on a broad and comprehensive scale it must be in the light of a recovery, and I do not think we could have done what we did do had it not been for the evidences to which the hon. gentleman has referred.
I will not anticipate the discussion on the resolution which appears on the order paper; that would be improper. But surely it is not intended to amend the constitution by asking the British parliament to enact retroactive legislation that could never find a place

in a people's constitution. It does seem to me extremely doubtful whether we should ask any -parliament to enact legislation of that sort. But when you say that you propose to clothe the provincial legislatures with power over indirect taxation, even though you limit, it, you have created a situation of the greatest gravity, one which we will discuss when we come to the resolution. As I say, I will not anticipate that discussion except to point out that as a result of what has transpired the province of Alberta did not accept the proposal made and has defaulted. And of course the effect will not be felt for some time. People who hold securities do not dump them on the market the next day or the next week or month; they await events. And it is the waiting on events that causes me to make a protest against a new proposal being made at this particular time.
