speechtext:
I know, but it is a new
proposal; and in dealing with financial matters, as I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me, there is nothing more destructive of credit than the lack of finality with respect to proposals that affect great bodies of people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I agree, but my night
hon. friend would be the first to admit that during the last five years arriving at finality, in finances, has been a difficult matter

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was exactly the
point I was endeavouring to make, by stating that I could not quite understand why the proposals made were modified as they were, having regard to the change that is contemplated in the constitution.
Having dealt with the financial situation, and the proposals that have been made from time to time and that have resulted, I think, in what the minister has very properly described as manifest evidences of recovery and in low rates of interest for our borrowings, I shall proceed to discuss shortly the proposals which he has made dealing with the tariff. But before I do that I think I should say a few words with respect to the debt. The hon, gentleman pointed out the other day that in the last six years there has been an addition of $867,000,000 to the national debt. That is undoubtedly quite correct. But $65,000,000 of that was for capital expenditures, and under the public works construction act something over $38,900,000 was expended, the reason being that on all sides in this bouse and in the country there was a continuous clamour for a public works program. A public works program could come

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
into being only if the money were provided for it, and the expenditure amounting to
138,905,000	that is mentioned as part of the national debt was incurred for that very purpose. Then, of that total of $887,000,000, you have these two items:	(a) Canadian
National Railways, $264,677,000; (b) Canadian National Railway and indirect, including the steamships, $40,310,000; making a total of about $305,000,000 that was borrowed for the purpose of maintaining these properties. Then we have .relief; that took $231,900,000, or substantially $232,000,000, more; and we wrote off dead assets, that is soldier settlement expenditure, $11000,000. That gives us, of the whole $867,000,000, a total of $652,000,000, leaving the deficits to be responsible for the balance, after adjustments, of $212,000,000. That is a yearly average, as will be observed of less than $40,000,000, and if there is added to that the whole of the contemplated loss with respect to wheat, that would make a total average of about $40,000,000 per annum during the last five years, the balance of the money being for the purposes I have indicated.
That in itself, having regard to conditions in Canada, is not an unfavourable result. I should be glad if it had only been S4,COO,COO or $400,000. But if in this vast country we were to keep people from starvation; if we were to care for the drought-stricken areas; if we were .to take care of what at one time amounted to over 300,000 people in one province receiving benefits; if we were to carry on relief for men, women and children numbering at one time nearly 1,300,000 souls, there is only one way in which this could be done, and that was through the utilization, in the manner intimated, of the credit of the dominion. If on the other hand we were to endeavour to supply employment, as we did, because a broad public works program was urged by this house, that too could be done only by money expended for the purpose. So there you have it both ways. You have the addition to the national debt; you have that money being utilized for relief, on the one hand, and. for work to prevent the necessity of relief, on the other. That is all I have to say with respect to the national debt, without going into it in detail as we may do l-ater on. Of course there was also the enormous item in connection with the railways and the steamships, amounting to over $300,000,000.
I desire to make one observation only with respect to the question of the tariff. When in 1931 we enacted legislation creating the tariff board, those who are students of histoiy
and will take the trouble to read Hansard of that day, particularly the observations of the right hon. the Prime Minister, will see some reason why the ridiculousness of the attitude taken then is apparent in the light of the performance to-day. This will be found in part in Hansard of October 17, 1932, and a later statement of it when certain changes were being made. We were dealing with the old country tariff. Members of the Liberal party of that day said that it was a scandal to have the country come and appeal to the tariff board. By legislation passed this session, all may do this. The Prime Minister said: if one, why not all? It is a matter of principle, so he has given the privilege to all. Second, we had the idea that the tariff board could not make recommendations. It does not; the statute does not give them power to do so. The minister the other day referred to their "recommendations"; I have them under my hand; and, Mr. Speaker, the tariff board do not make recommendations; they do just what the act says; they find the facts and then they find the tariff which would be necessary to give to Canadians an equal opportunity with those from the outside who might be their competitors. Take, for instance, the automobile industry, reference No. 91. That matter was referred to the tariff board by the late government, not by the present government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I said so.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. The proceedings
were protracted, and finally the board gave judgment. In that judgment they set out existing conditions and they set out what in their judgment would be a tariff that would meet the situation which was presented by the users of automobiles in the country. The governments of the various provinces were represented; others also were represented; they made their cases, and as a result the government has adopted that as its tariff to-day. I cannot find a single change in it. So far as I can see, the tariff as written in the resolutions with reference to automobiles is the judgment of the board as to the kind of tariff which it would be necessary to pass to meet the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is just one difference.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which one is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The difference is the suggestion that the government should take power to increase the tariff. That suggestion-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I had reference only to the actual enactments and not to the question
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

of suggestions as to what might or might not be done. The government never take power by order in council to increase the tariff; they can always lower it, but never increase it. But the judgment of the board (a) as to the facts and (b) as to the tariff which should be enacted to meet the situation provided by the act, namely that Canadians should have equal opportunity with others, is found now in the resolutions that have been introduced in the house.
Take the next items, artificial silk yarns, forged steel rolls, rhinestones and metals, photographic appliances and equipment; all those are items that have been placed on the resolutions now before the house, and not by other than the tariff board's consideration. The tariff board that was so roundly condemned a few short years ago is now accepted as the proper tribunal to deal with this matter. I desire only to point out that with respect to gasoline, which was referred to the board by the predecessor of the present Minister of Finance, there is a masterly review of the whole situation, a finding of the facts and then a statement that a certain operation would bring about a certain result, namely the equalization, using the word in a broad sense, of opportunity between those inside and those outside this country. That is, owing to conditions to which reference is made, Canadians would be enabled to have an equal opportunity. But before I leave the automobile industry there is just one point that I desire to place on Hansard, because I think it is very important. The effort to secure lower freight rates is referred to, and in chapter V of this report they say:
The board is of the opinion that the existing methods of distribution of automobiles in Canada are unnecessarily wasteful.
In chapter IV of this report the board reviewed the condition with respect to the used car problem and indicated the seriousness of the situation arising out of the unjustifiable allowances made on second hand automobiles. The board, in that chapter, also mentioned that the losses made by dealers on the automobiles taken in trade tend to increase with the net amount of commission allowed on the sale of a new car and, from the facts before the board it is evident that dealers receiving high commissions are the ones most disposed to overbid on used cars traded in, with resultant demoralization of the market.
It would appear, therefore, that it might be expedient for the automobile manufacturers, if they are intent on correcting the above abuses, to reduce existing discounts and to establish-after consultation among themselves-a policy of uniform all-embracing dealers' discounts which would eliminate extra payment to their dealers, referred to in chapter III, in the shape of profit on freight or handling and other charges.
The board is of the opinion that the industry, if it would carry into practice the

suggestions made above, would in time correct some of the major ills existing in the marketing of automobiles and at the same time effect substantial economies that should be passed on to the Canadian consumer.
Then they refer to the provincial governments and the representations made by them as to the necessity of having reduced transportation charges on cars to the respective provinces, and they say:
The board indicated that the selling price in Canada of copper and lead of Canadian origin sold to automobile and automotive parts manufacturers is substantially higher than the price at which these same metals are being sold for export by the Canadian producers.
I see in the budget no evidence of any attempt to remedy that situation, and I think it is high time that it was remedied. I certainly made some effort in that direction, and the former Minister of Finance endeavoured to do so, but nothing except drastic legislation will accomplish that end. I think it is high time that we who are doing so much to assist the provinces and the dominion should see to it that there is no discrimination against Canadian consumers with' respect to metals produced in our own country. That was placed very clearly before the board.
Then, in view of this finding, there is one other matter in connection with which I think legislation should be enacted at this session. This is not a new matter, and would have been dealt with last session but for the fact that the matter was being referred to the board.
The board is of the opinion that wholly owned Canadian subsidiaries of foreign automobile corporations should be requested to publish annually their balance sheets and financial statements to the same extent as public Canadian companies. This^ seems to the board to be specially advisable in the case of corporations seeking and obtaining tariff protection for their products.
I think that can be easily accomplished by an amendment to the Companies Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is under consideration.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Bennett
anyway. When the other day I saw part of the advertising in connection with this very propaganda to have the reduction made, and when I saw the photograph of an industry in 1911 and the great and magnificent structure in 1936, I did not give much consideration to the cries of poverty which will be put up by that industry, and neither would anybody else. I repeat that that is a feature of the budget calculated in every possible way to be unfair to Canadian producers.
There is another feature of the budget about which I should like to speak, namely countervailing duties. I do not make the statement offensively when I say that countervailing duties represent the cowardice of an administration not prepared to raise the duty. They are frightened, because they say that it is contrary to their general policy, although they admit that under the present budget they have raised the duties in some instances. But look at this: Eggs, cut flowers and potatoes are under countervailing duties. Yes, eggs, flowers and potatoes are under countervailing duties.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They have come back, after six years.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes; the eggs are pretty stale; the flowers are wilted and the potatoes have sprouted. Let us look at these countervailing duties. As between the United States and Canada, these duties were first set up by the United States and the effect of them was to destroy the market in nearby states for Alberta coal. Making it applicable to the whole country they said, "If a country has a higher duty than we have with respect to coal, then the coal which comes in from Canada must carry a higher rate." The result was that coal from Lethbridge was denied a market in certain parts of the United States.
We tried countervailing provisions in 1930, and now rather than raise the duty frankly, rather than just raise it and say, "Our duty is so and so on eggs, flowers and potatoes," what do we do- We say, "The existing duty is two cents on eggs, but inasmuch as you reduce your duty to two cents, we are going to have the same rate of duty as you have, which is ten cents a dozen."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is all right.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
With 130,000,000 people in the United States and 11,000,000 people in Canada? Countervailing duties existing between this country and a great people 130,000,000 strong, with climatic conditions about which we know nothing, a people growing flowers, raising potatoes and producing eggs! And, mark you, this applies to other coun-

tries as well. It applies to China. What is the duty on eggs going into China? Are we now to be supplied with Chinese eggs, such as we received some years ago? Is that to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman knows better than that.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not; it is a fact. I know that in this country for purposes of production of confectionery large quantities of eggs came to Canada from China. So far I have been unable to ascertain what the Chinese duty is, but I think the Chinese duty is no higher than ours. Therefore, if the Chinese duty is nothing we shall be subject to competition from Chinese eggs at two cents a dozen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In that case it does not change our duty in the slightest degree.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, but what it does is this: It says that we shall not make our tariff, but that if the United States will place a duty of two cents on eggs we shall place ours at two cents, knowing all the time that congress has not been dealing' with tariffs; knowing all the time that the president has no power to reduce the duty, and knowing that under the provisions of the law he can reduce it to only five cents. Is this not just a gigantic gesture which means nothing? The minister knows that the president cannot deal with the tariffs. He knows that congress is not dealing with tariffs at this session, and he therefore must know that this is absolutely nugatory, so far as results are concerned. The same applies to the 40 per cent rate on cut flowers.
The other day the hon. member said that we had left no tariff for the intermediate and the British preference, and neither we had. They were free. They were intended to be free, and 40 per cent was the general tariff. The United States was then under the general tariff. When we changed and gave the United States the intermediate tariff, the simple thing, having reserved our right to do so, was to place a reasonable duty against cut flowers and eggs. They have a 40 per cent rate against us. We are to have a 40 per cent rate. That is the position. Is that the idea of Canada's nationhood?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because flowers go both ways; so do potatoes, and so do eggs.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes; I notice, though, that baby chicks are taken care of.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Because they do not go both ways.

The Budget-Mr. Bennett

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They do not go both ways?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think that is hardly correct, but they do not go in substantial quantities. But to say to the Canadian people that we have to buy eggs from the United States and that there is a two-way traffic in them is a straining of words, because relatively speaking we buy very few eggs from the United States.
So far as cut flowers are concerned we have this simple point to consider: We have a country of which the major part is in the north temperate zone. In the United States are found varieties of climates, and as a result they can produce when we cannot. Eggs, and early potatoes at 75 cents-the minister and every hon. member must know that, congress cannot deal with these, because congress is not dealing with tariffs at this session. The effect of this is what, so far as we are concerned? It is to place a duty of 10 cents on eggs, 40 per cent on flowers and 75 cents on potatoes.
Then we come to one further point in the budget, namely the statement made by the minister with respect to the mining industry. I want to ask a question with regard to a clause which comes to me as not a wholly new recommendation. A year ago the government of the day provided for the development of^ the mining industry by appropriating a million dollars for such development. But when the price of gold was raised from S20.67 to $35 per ounce, the government of that day, knowing that this was not a provincial matter and had been brought about not by provincial but by national happenings, took steps to collect part of the money, and did collect it. I know of no reason why one industry should be singled out for freedom from taxation. But for a moment let us see how the minister puts it. His statement at page 2386 of Hansard is a wonderful one, because it is so seldom one has an opportunity to read on the records of this house a statement of this kind. These are his words:
I desire to add that as uncertainty of taxation is a definite deterrent to the making of new commitments in a hazardous industry, the mining industry may rely upon it that this government will not impose discriminatory taxation with respect to mines.
We will all agree with that. He continues:
While the present government is in power, mining enterprises can depend upon treatment at least as favourable as that accorded to other industries under the corporation income tax.
Now I want to ask this question:	Will
the minister say that all other industries in 12739-161}
Canada will receive treatment as favourable as that accorded to the mining industry? Will he say that? If not, why not? Let us look and see what has happened. Take the income tax imposed against the profits of a mine; whether it was rich or not, whether it had greater reserves or not, fifty per cent of the profits was free from taxation and the 124 per cent corporation tax was reckoned only on one-half. That is, if the profit was $2,000,000, the tax was 124 per cent on $1,000,000. But that was not all. When the dividend went into the hands of the shareholder, the shareholder before he paid his income tax, deducted fifty per cent from his dividend on the ground of exhaustion and depletion,	and	some	of	these mines,according to their own published statements, had reserves ample to take care of anything that might arise for from thirty-five to	fifty	years.	So	we cutthe exemption	d-own to	33J	per	cent as
regards the corporation tax and to 20 per cent on behalf of the shareholders, and of course we incurred much enmity for that. We were abused, and I think we paid a rather high price for 'it.
But, sir, let us have a clear understanding. Is it not right	and	just	and	fair	that, so
far as possible, everybody in Canada should stand equal under our taxation laws? That is what we endeavoured to do. I am wholly in accord with the minister's willingness to grant exemption from income tax at the start to those who may be engaged in this hazardous undertaking, but I point out that he must do something to prevent

he cannot prevent it but he must see to it that the provinces do-this wild speculation that takes place, which sweeps away the earnings of a lifetime and makes paupers in the end of those who speculate. I get letters every day, as the minister does, with respect to this, and surely something must be done about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I must say that the
provinces are doing a great deal.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To start with Alberta;
that province passed a law which was held intra vires by the privy council, and its action was followed by other provinces. This does a great deal to prevent abuses in that regard. But when a minister makes a statement of this kind:
While the present government is in power, mining enterprises can depend upon treatment at least as favourable as that accorded to other industries under tile corporation income tax.
The converse of that should equally be said, that while he is in office other corpora-
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

tions will receive the treatment as favourable as that accorded ito the mining industry. That will involve the necessary investigation of the situation for the purpose of determining to what extent provision has been made by way of reserves and otherwise for the return of capital and the continued existence of the enterprise itself.
Now I come for a moment to what the minister proposes for the purpose of raising the revenue necessary for carrying on government. Two methods may be pursued: (a) economies, and (b) taxation. The minister may effect further economies, if they can be effected, or he can place the burden by taxation on the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or borrow.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is the same thing;
that is what I mean by taxation. Or he may combine both. He said the other day that the government are investigating the question of economies. One of the first things that the late government had to do was to make investigations in connection with that very matter. But, Mr. Speaker, I am not at all impressed with the great sincerity of the government when the minister talks about the question of economies, for I hold in my hand the report of the civil service commission down to the end of 1935'-I have not the report for 1936-and I find on page 9 how much we actually spent in this countiy to keep the machine going. In round figures we spent in 1925 and subsequent years the following:
1925		 $74,200,000
1926		 74,600.000
1927		 76.200.000
1928		 82.300.000
1929		 S7.500.000
1930		 90.800,000
1931		 94,300,000
That is the year for which we did not budget, the year 1931 prior to March 31.
1932		 $92,500,000
1933		 79.500.000
1934		 77,100.000
1935		 74,460,000
That was necessary to take care of a grand total of permanent and other employees of 38.946 in 1925, 45.581 in 1931, and 40,792 in 1935.
We did succeed in effecting some economies. We did succeed in making it clear beyond peradventure that the country was overstaffed, but I cannot seriously regard the minister's statement of his desire to effect economies when I find a position in the chief electoral officer's office which was vacant when we came into office, and which had not been filled

because there was nothing to do, filled after the election of which Mr. Castonguay took charge by the son of the president of the Liberal Association in Ottawa. After the election he was appointed to that position as assistant to Mr. Castonguay. Can it be explained what he has to do? Can anybody tell us what he has to do? If for nine years there was no necessity for such an appointment, why has that appointment been made? Take the case of Brigadier Caldwell, who had taken his retiring allowance and was about to leave the service, who had taken his six months' leave. We find him appointed master general of the ordnance, a position which had not been filled since the death of General Morrison, and that was years ago.
I think the people of this country like myself will not regard these proceedings as evidence of any serious desire to economize. How many have been added to the service since October 23 last? It is true that this government has displaced nearly every man who held a position and could be displaced by appointing someone favourable to the administration. That we understand, and I am not complaining or cavilling at it. But how many additional men have been placed in positions in the civil service, and why should we discuss this question of taxation or economies until we have dealt with the great problem that is connected with economies? Part of these economies were brought, about by the ten per cent and then the five per cent deduction in salaries. I recall that my hon. friends opposite complained in bitterest terms about that economy, but I notice that they continue the five per cent deduction this year by special enactment.
The point I desire to make is this: The minister is confronted with a crisis, and no one knows that better than I. I do not say this in any boasting sense, but I have a clear appreciation of the difficulties of the minister, and I sympathize with him and am willing to do anything I reasonably can to assist him in his difficulties. But I say this, that he has a stupendous task, and we cannot save Canada unless we are prepared to hew to the line and make sacrifices on a scale such as were made by the old country when they formed the government in 1931. I know that hon. gentlemen opposite with their great majority are in a position to do anything. Never in the history of this country has a government been so situated, and that is why I congratulate the first minister upon the steps taken at the very opening of the session with respect to all these matters. He had to do it.
When I say to the minister that in my judgment an eight per cent sales tax is one

The Budget-Mr. Bennett
which Canada cannot bear, I but reflect the opinion of at least two or three former ministers of finance. We all know that Mr. Fielding thought the country could stand a higher tax than six per cent, but he found out it could not and he had to get the tax back to six per cent. We know what succeeding men have done. The minister succeeded in reducing the tax to one per cent in 1930, but does he think the capitalist system can survive with an eight per cent tax? I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr Woodsworth) must have rejoiced when he heard this budget, because he knows, as I know, that nothing will strike a greater blow at the whole capitalist system than an eight per cent sales tax. The price of small automobiles goes up S18. All we have to do is realize that the sales tax is one-third greater than it was. Just reckon up what that means Hon. gentlemen have seen the operation of sales taxes in the provinces and in some of the states of the American union. New Jersey employed this tax and the city of New York imposed one to deal with unemployment relief matters. These were turn-over taxes; no matter if your purchase was only a cent, you had to pay the tax by means of a token. That was found to be an onerous tax, but one that produced large sums of money.
Can this country stand an eight per cent sales tax? In my judgment it cannot. I have given as much thought to this as I can, because I have no desire to interpose any objections to the efforts made by the government to do what it is so anxious to do, namely, to establish an equilibrium between income and outgo. But we must face the facts frankly. I do not see how this dominion from what I know of its economic structure, can stand an eight per cent sales tax. This is a tremendous tax. It is a tax which the minister's predecessors felt could not safely be imposed. It will be recalled that considerable discussion was held as to whether this rate could not be increased, but we got down to six per cent as the maximum. I am bound to say that there were those who suggested that the rate should be higher than six pet cent. The former Minister of Finance, the Hon. Mr. Rhodes, looked into the matter with great care. I believe there are men in the department wrho believe that an eight per cent tax is sound; that the tax could be increased 33,1 per cent, but I cannot see how this country under present conditions can stand an eight per cent sales tax.
There was one other tax about which I used to hear a great deal, the tax of one cent a pound on sugar. I wonder how many hon. members promised that that was going to disappear just as soon as the first budget came along?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We did not have to make promises the last time.	.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not discussing that phase of the matter now; I am only pointing out that that was so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nothing would give me greater pleasure than to put it where it was.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister has indicated in his answer just what I desired to say. At the close of his speech the minister said that the government were making a conscientious effort to grapple with the problem. May I say that he has no monopoly in that regard. For five years men quite as honest and almost as capable as he were endeavouring to deal with the same problem. In dealing with these problems, if it became necessary to have some certainty with respect to revenue, you must tax something that is of universal consumption and will produce a certain revenue. I agree with the minister when he says that nothing would give him greater pleasure than to remove that tax if he could, but he cannot. But I do not think this argument applies with respect to the eight per cent sales tax. There are other methods, which it is not my duty or privilege to discuss, by which the situation might be met. I can conceive of nothing more disastrous to the capitalist system; I can conceive of nothing that will impose greater hardship and difficulty upon the people of Canada than an endeavour to collect an eight per cent sales tax.
The allegation is made that our tariffs are going to be reduced in order to lessen the cost to the consumer. I have endeavoured to point out that that will not accomplish any such purpose. To the extent that business goes from Canada, to the same extent is lessened the ability of this country to survive. That is quite obvious.
The hon. gentleman has provided for a deficit with respect to wheat and oats extending over a period of five or six years. He knows as well as I do, that the guarantees given to the banks are against ultimate loss and until there has been a liquidation of these stocks, that amount cannot be determined. It must be determined when there has been an ultimate liquidation. The banks were willing to accept a guarantee which provided for the payment of an ultimate loss. Whatever that ultimate loss may be, this is not the time or the place to discuss what I believe to be the ill-conceived policy of the government with respect to wheat. I cannot discuss that at the moment as this may be done at another time. It is the ultimate
The Budget-Mr. Bennett

liability or loss that was guaranteed and until such time as that is determined, why anticipate it in this budget or in any other?

That is the idea of the hon. member. How can the people of this country ever appreciate this problem if members of this house, responsible members, say it is purely political.
I close, sir, with this note, because of all the problems confronting the dominion to-day there is not one that is so serious, none fraught with graver possibilities of disaster. There is not one problem more critical than that connected with the railway situation. This problem will not wait; it should not wait. A government fresh from the people and having shown courage to deal with some of the problems in the manner in which they have done, for which I have given them such commendation as it is possible for me to give, should not wait longer to deal with this problem. For it is not a problem that can be solved by the substitution of one man for another. It calls for a bold and determined course, to get to the very bottom of the matter, so that this country may continue, as the minister says, its progress towards recovery. It has made progress; that has been admitted by the minister in stronger terms than I would have used had I been indicating it myself. There is an indication of a reward of the efforts that men made during five long years when they gave their best to the state in which they live and which they serve. But we have now reached the stage where, unless we are prepared to deal heroically with the cancer that is gnawing at the very vitals of our national life, I do not think we can continue our progress towards recovery, and that for two reasons: first, because our credit will suffer and the minister will be confronted with difficulties the magnitude of which he contemplates but does not care even to mention; and, second, because it will bring disaster to confederation itself and destroy the very fabric of this dominion.
Mr. J. II. BLACKMORE (Lethbridge): In rising to take part, in this debate I should like first of all to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) for this budget. I regarded it as having been carefully studied and very well arranged, and it was given to the house in good form and with a clear and pleasing delivery, which seems to be a rare thing in this house. I did not find in this budget evidence of that progressiveness of outlook which I believed the people of Can-

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
ada were justified in expecting of the Liberal party. There are in evidence no changes of policy for the future. The budget, I feel impelled to say, is reactionary and strictly of the old order. The great problem for us and for Canada at the present time is that of getting purchasing power into the consumers' hands. This budget actually is designed to take purchasing power out of the consumers' hands. This it does by an exceedingly painful sales tax, and we know that a sales tax is the most effective means of tapping, shall we say, the purchasing power of every individual, particularly the poor and those who are struggling with small incomes and endeavouring to raise families and carry on the responsibilities of life. It is precisely in this class that we must have the purchasing power. While I do not blame the Minister of Finance for getting money where he can, I deplore this as a definite means of taking purchasing power away from the very people in whose hands purchasing power should be, and, I contend, must be, if this country is ever to recover its economic stability.
I noticed that there was no plan designed to replace this purchasing power either immediately or ultimately. As I see it, the great thing we require at this time is monetary reform. I heard a good deal of the propaganda which our Liberal friends used throughout the last election, and read a good deal of what appeared in the press. As a result of- all that I was encouraged to believe that there was to be monetary reform; that the Liberal party was committed to it. I therefore came here expecting to find that very early after this parliament assembled, definite and progressive steps would be made towards monetary reform. Either no such steps are being taken, or my vision is too thoroughly dulled to enable me to see them. Monetary reform must take two forms: First of all, a method of obtaining money without interest and without debt; second, a method of distributing the money so that it can get into the consumer's hands.
We are living among changed conditions. I deprecate therefore the tendency to continue as though we shall be able to get out of this depression, as people have come out of previous depressions, by natural, normal means. I feel distinctly alarmed, as the previous speaker also expressed himself, because I do not find evidence that we are in normal conditions. I find no evidence that we are, as Stuart Chase tells me that people were, in previous depressions; rather the indications seem to be that we are in conditions such as our fathers have never known.

A number of men, I find, have a similar idea to this. May I draw to the attention of the house some studies which have been made recently in the capitalistic system. I hold no opposition whatsoever towards the capitalistic system. Just the same, we must be warned when signs of decay such as are here indicated are brought to our attention, Mr. Arthur H. Adams, in an article called Key Ratio to Balance, appearing in the American Federationist magazine, November, 1934, makes a definite contribution to the study of the present system as we are experiencing it to-day. He uses a fraction. He makes the numerator of that fraction the real wages of consumer goods workers, and the denominator he makes by taking the output per man hour. It is designed to be a scientific critical study of conditions as they are. He finds that real wages must increase as fast as productivity. Now, sir, this is the very condition which we find no longer exists in our economic life, either in the United States or in Canada. He finds that if his ratio, arrived at by his fraction, falls to 90 per cent the economic life of the country is in danger; if it falls to 75 per cent, the economic system is unworkable. In 1922 his ratio was 100, which is normal; in 1929 his ratio was 73, which was impossible, and in 1934 his ratio was 75. I neglected to say that these figures are based upon conditions in the United States. Our country is economically so closely knit to the United States that I assume conditions are very much the same here. He uses these words in commenting upon his findings:
The unbalance we have reached this time is so big that natural or automatic restoration of balance, or recovery, cannot occur. The buying power of all consumer goods workers in the United States needs to be raised about 35 per cent on the average, and with no increase in their producing power, before an intelligent man should even hope for business to become self-sustaining at normal levels.
Hon. members will find the investigation described in Stuart Chase's fine book, Government in Business, at page 99.
Another student of the situation Chase says is a man named A. A. Berle, Junior. This man published his findings in a book called Liquid Claims and National Wealth, published by the Macmillan Company in 1934. He has an entirely unique and startling way of attacking the problem, but he feels that it is thoroughly worth considering. He discovers, in going back over past years, that the amount of liquid money existing in a community has a definite bearing upon the stability of that community. He finds, for example, that in

The Budget*-Mr. Blackmore
1880 sixteen per cent of the total wealth of the United States was liquid. Of course we all know that "liquid" means money which is readily available through bank deposits or through the sale of gilt-edged bonds and the like. In 1912, he found that twenty per cent of the money was liquid. In 1926 he found that the percentage was twenty-eight per cent. You notice, Mr. Speaker, a most alarming rise there, indicating that new conditions were developing the like of which man never saw before. In 1929 he found that the percentage was thirty-eight per cent; that was the year of the depression. In 1930 it was forty per cent. In 1933, notwithstanding the heroic efforts which were put forth to recover conditions in the United States, thirty-four per cent, or one-third of the national wealth, was found to be liquid. He makes this general observation, that if a country has fifteen per cent of its wealth liquid it can weather a depression, but if it has twenty per cent liquid its chances of weathering that depression are very slight. He makes this statement:
It was a stampede for liquidity which closed every bank in 1933, a phenomenon unheard of in any former depression.
This will be found recorded in the book of Stuart Chase to which I referred before, at page 102.	_	_
Another interesting study of this situation, scientifically conducted, is that by Professor Rautenstrauch, of Columbia university. He approaches the question again from another most unexpected angle; he finds that in 1917 producers among the workers of the United States comprised sixty-three per cent of the total employed. That is, the farmers, the miners and the men who were producing totalled sixty-three per cent of those employed, and they received one-half of the national income. But in 1932 see the surprising change that has taken place; he finds that fifty per cent of the employed were producers and that they received only one-third of the national income. In other words the producers had dropped from sixty-three per cent to fifty per cent of the total employed between 1917 and 1932, and instead of receiving one-half of the national income they received only one-third. This is an alarming change in such a few years, and again indicates that it is doubtful whether we can get out of this depression by normal means. Professor Rautenstrauch according to Chase has this to say:
In other words, in 1917, when producers got one dollar for making goods, overhead people got another dollar for the various services leading up to the sale of goods to the consumer. But in 1932, when producers got one dollar, overheaders got $2.30. In 1929 they
got $1.60. Overhead costs marched rapidly forward during the 1920's, and broke into a run with the coming of the depression. Business on the down grade; overhead on the up grade-Here is abundant evidence of shocking management.	_	_
If the ratios between direct and indirect labour were about right in 1917, to recapture them we should now need to:
1.	Shift 12,300,000 more workers to the producers' group.
2.	Increase producers' income about 56 per cent.
3.	Increase farmers' income about 216 per cent-as their proportionate share in the producers' group.
Again, Mr. Speaker, this outline was discussed at page 104 of Stuart Chase's book Government in Business. Let me repeat that according to Chase the article I have just read was by Professor Rautenstrauch, entitled Who Gets the Money, appearing in Harper's Magazine in 1934. This is a serious situation indeed. It does not by any means indicate that hon. members on either side of this house are justified in taking this matter calmly. Rather it indicates that we should be bestirring ourselves with a great deal of energy, not expecting to go sliding along on a laissez faire policy. Unless we bestir ourselves we are going to be held accountable by an indignant people who sent us here to make things right.
Now let me refer to another serious matter which has been discussed in this house many times. I refer to technological unemployment. I have a number of excerpts dealing with that question which, with your permission, sir, I should like to quote. The first comes from Stuart Chase's pamphlet Technocracy, an Interpretation, at page 15:
From 1912 to 1917 the Buick Motor Company increased its production 1,400 per cent and its labour force only 10 per cent.
I intend to quote these excerpts, which I have found at random in my reading, because a number of people are disposed to smile at these changes which have arisen, thinking they will pass by. These signs which I have found do not indicate any justification whatever for any such optimism. In The Problem of Unemployment, at page 122, Paul H. Douglas says:
There were in 1929 approximately 500,000 or nearly six per cent fewer wage earners in manufacturing than there had been a decade before, while there were 300,000 or 15 per cent fewer workers on the railways.
Notice that these figures are taken from the period before the depression; consequently we must look upon them as being drawn from normal times such as we hope will return. My next quotation is from Stuart Chase's

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
book Men and Machines, at page 210, where 1 found the following words of interest:
The decline in 1929 registers over 2,000,000 and all recent counts of factory workers show a greater output with not only relatively, but absolutely, fewer men. For a hundred years every census tabulated an increasing number of persons employed in factories; now suddenly since the war, with an increasing population, there are fewer persons in factories. Something cardinal has happened; some mighty corner has been rounded.
That is exactly my contention. Let us be well advised before taking too much for granted. Something cardinal has happened; some mighty corner has been rounded. The next extract which I found of interest also comes from Stuart Chase's book Men and Machines, at page 210:
Evans Clark in the New York Times shows the phenomenon by index numbers.
