subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I was proceeding to show how changed are conditions confronting us from those which confronted our fathers when previous depressions occurred, and I was making reference to the technological unemployment which exists in our civilization to-day, largely as a result of the development of machinery. I had cited evidence from certain authorities to show that we had turned some mighty corner. Going on with the evidence to bear out this contention let me cite the following from page 214 of Men and Machines by Stuart Chase:

Mr. Ethelbert Stewart, a most qualified observer, sees the higher level of unemployment in the spring of 1928 as perhaps only the beginning of a more or less permanent unemployment, because a growing number of industries are equipped to produce more than consumers have money to buy, together with the supplanting of workers by machines.
Quoting again from page 214 I read:
Mr. Horace Taylor is sure that "all evidences point to a steadily increasing technological unemployment," and many competent economists agree with him.
Before I proceed further may I point out that a considerable amount of disagreement exists, and there is a tendency to quote one authority against another. Making all due allowances for all just differences of opinion I believe we are safe in assuming what the testimony of these men tends to bear out. Quoting from Technocracy, an Interpretation, page 30, I read;
The automobile industry created 4,000,000 new jobs out of thin air. There is no such industry on the horizon.
In other words, although by reference to certain industries such as the automotive industry, we can see some evidence that new machines create new jobs-and a great deal of argument is adduced to show that this is so far true as to justify a great deal of optimism-notwithstanding that fact, unemployed continue to exist in terrifying numbers.
As an example of a man who argues that increased machinery does produce new jobs we might mention William J. Cameron of the Ford Motor Company, whose article is printed at page 4 of the March 25 issue of the Christian Science Monitor. His message is that going back over forty years the evidence tends to show that machinery has increased the number of jobs. It is strange to observe that against this man's contention all the evidence I have cited to-night bears overwhelmingly. It may be true that a large number of new jobs are created by new machinery. For example, when the automobile business developed we know the garage business had a corresponding development. But we shall find that the displacement of men is not equalled by the replacement of men. So frequently do the new jobs require so little of men's time and so quickly are machines developed to take the place of men that I feel quite certain we are justified in going forward upon the assumption that there will be in our civilization a permanent technological unemployment which must be met by adjustments in our economic behaviour sufficient for the occasion.

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
Another serious evidence that we are in a changed condition is to be found by reference to agriculture. A few days ago I made a citation, but there were so few in the house I shall impose upon the good nature of hon. members to the extent of reciting it again to-night. Quoting from Government in Business by Stuart Chase I find this startling information at page 39:
Even in such a prosperous year as 1927, "Recent Economic Changes" shows a net loss of $1,717,000,000 to farmers as a class, a loss enormously accelerated by the depression. Agriculture has failed as a self-sustaining sector of private business.
If these considerations I have adduced are not sufficient to show that we are living in changed conditions which have brought upon us an alarming new situation, then I simply have not the power to draw sound conclusions. Notwithstanding all of this there is no cause for great alarm, provided we go forward to meet the situation calmly and sanely, and do not assume that it will right itself. Although the patient is desperately sick it is possible to perform an operation which will save his life, if we approach the problem in time and with sufficient skill.
In the first place there is no need for poverty. Throughout this dominion, sir, there is absolutely no need for it, and any government which continues to permit poverty either does not know what to do or is not trying to find out. We have plenty of food; we can produce, in greater abundance than we need, practically all the food we can consume. Lately I have found among hon. members the disposition to argue academically about this matter. But on this occasion let us appeal to common sense.	Is there any
hon. member who questions that Canada can raise all the wheat she wants? Not a soul. Does anyone question that she can produce all other grains she needs? Not a soul. Or that she can produce grain products such as flour, oatmeal and the like? Not a soul. It is absurd to make such a suggestion, is it not? Will anyone argue seriously that we cannot produce all the beef, pork, mutton and other meats that we need? It is absurd to raise that question, is it not? Will any person doubt our ability to produce all the dairy products such as butter, milk and cream that we need? If we were unable to do so we would find the prices of these products at something like a living rate, instead of at a level so low that they are driving men out of production. Will anyone seriously question our ability to produce all the potatoes we need, or to produce all other vegetables we require? Can we not produce the greater portion of the fruits we require?
While we are not so abundantly equipped for the production of fruits, yet our production is surprising.
Turning from that to clothing we know that certainly we can produce all the woollen goods we require, all the shoes we need and a wide variety of other articles of clothing. Therefore there is no need of any lack of clothing, even if there are some things we cannot produce. Will anyone seriously question our ability to produce all necessary shelter? We have an abundance of building material, and no person would attempt to question our ability to build. Right here in this Canada of ours all we need is to set men to work to produce those needs. Is there anyone who will seriously question our ability to produce all the fuel we need to keep us warm? Think of the vast coal fields of Alberta and other sections of the country. It is simply absurd to suppose that we cannot produce all the fuel we need in Canada. Again, we are able to produce all the entertainment we need. Why should our people go without entertainment in this country?
I turn to education and culture. Surely we can get in this dominio'n all the education we want. We have our teachers and our schools. Why cannot we ge,t all the education and culture we need in Canada? It- is here, and what we have not here we can soon get through the intelligent people we have.
Again, our transportation facilities are abundant. No one should want for transportation in this country, equipped as we are.
Take health and other services. The means of obtaining these things are here. Numbers of men are to-day unemployed who could doctor our children and do their dental work. Why should we not have health service?
I contend, Mr. Speaker, that in the light of present day conditions it is utterly absurd that we should even seriously contemplate the idea of having poverty in this land. The question is: How are we going to proceed to the solution of the difficulty, because there are manifest difficulties in getting this plenty available? There is a reason why. For a number of years we have been much concerned over the causes of this depression, but most of the authorities whom I have read are now agreed that the cause of all the trouble is money. It centres right around that one thing, money, and the question how we can get the money, and, second, how can we get it into the hands of the people who need it, are the two great questions that face this parliament and the country to-day. Most of the men whom 1 have studied are of opinion that we can have national money issued nationally. If we are afraid to issue national money lest the banks

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
might get it, and on the basis of that national money extend credit to dangerous proportions, thereby risking inflation, we can issue national credit. May I quote a few statements from a man whose standing must be recognized in this house. I know that a great many members look with a certain amount of indulgence and smiles upon the social credit people, thinking us somewhat crazy, but I am now going to quote someone whom I think everyone in this house will treat seriously, the Hon. Robert L. Owen, senator of the United States, living in Washington, D.C. He has been, I am told, director of a United States bank for forty-six years, and president of a bank for ten years. There is a man, I submit, who ought to know something of what he is talking about, and the words he utters we can safely give credence to. In his article entitled, Money, appearing in the Instructor for April, 1936, I read on page 54:
- It is the failure of governments to discharge their constitutional duty of regulating the value of money, including bank money, which has caused the enormous disaster from which we have recently suffered.
This gentleman is prominent in the monetary movements of President Roosevelt. While many may question President Roosevelt's wisdom, we may one day wake up to find that he is a long way ahead of anyone else in the Anglo-Saxon world in the matter of monetary reform; at least, there is a serious chance that he may be so. I quote from the same article, at page 60:
When one-half of our money supply is destroyed, it means that one-half of the market price of American property is destroyed. It is of supreme importance that the administration and its advisers should clearly understand the necessity for expanding the money supply until working capital is made available to the small business enterprises in sufficient volume to restore to employment the unemployed millions who still walk the streets unable to sell their labour at any price.
Again, at page 87, I read:
When the government creates an adequate supply of money to furnish all the working capital required by our people for transacting the business possible in this country, under favourable circumstances, there would be available the money that is needed, with which to employ all employable people and pay them good wages for reasonable hours.
Again, at page 92, I read:
A study and the understanding of money, how it is manufactured, and by whom; the study of constitutional money created by governments and how governments can regulate its value, is a solemn patriotic duty resting upon every adult citizen, more particularly members of governments, federal, state, .provincial and municipal.

There is no doubt in. that man's mind, is there? I contend that the solution of the problem which confronts us lies somewhere along the path of money. I know there is a good deal of easy merriment about the matter and a good deal of discussion whether it would not produce inflation and all that sort of thing. It is a good deal like irrigation. I come from a land where they irrigate. Unless you are careful in applying the water to your land, you will wash your young plants away and destroy your soil, but if you use irrigation as it should be used, expertly, wisely applied, it is a blessing. It gives the plants ju9t the thing they need to grow. I't is so with money power. If you use it with wisdom it will do no harm; it will be a blessing. Only when unwisely used does it cause trouble.
Of course, in order to make sure that this inflation or abuse of new money will not occur, the banks would have to be controlled to prevent inflation. I maintain that one of the duties of this government, a thing which I expected it to do and which it may yet do for all I know, for the session is not yet ended, is to appoint a banking commission to investigate the whole banking situation and determine the absolute truth about our money needs, so that the government may be prepared to handle banking and money scientifically. In addition, I think this government should begin to plan and encourage industry where industry is needed. There are many processes which could be introduced into this country. Processing plants could be established that would be of manifold advantage to the Canadian people, producing the things we need. There are for instance, the potato processing plants that I referred to the other night. Think of the tremendous advantage that coal processing would be to those coal areas where miners are to-day languishing in unemployment. It would change the whole aspect of the country, and we should be able to produce an abundance of goods which we are now importing, thereby helping to bring upon ourselves an unfavourable trade balance. We could introduce more sugar factories, but all I have seen anyone do since I oarne here is to put blocks in the way of the sugar industry. Canada produces only fourteen per cent of the sugar she needs. Where would we foe an case of war? Why should we not ourselves produce all the sugar we need, in case of difficulty? Why are we not doing this? Those are just a few samples of what we could do. There are mills for processing trees and pro-

The Budget-Mr. Hayhurst
cesses of many other kinds which would enable us to help ourselves and help us use a new money system more safely.
Why should we not have in this country a Canadian Brookings Institute to provide us with the actual economic facts about Canada? You cannot quote in this country a book that people will accept because there is nothing to tie it up to, and so we have to quote from figures in the United States. I say that that condition does not reflect credit on the Canadian people. We have men in Canada intelligent enough to find out these things for ourselves.
Having once established a system of getting new money, I contend, Mr. Speaker, that the day is coming when we must unquestionably have scientifically planned methods of getting the money into the hands of the people. I know there are plenty who laugh at that kind of thing, but before I sit down let me quote one set of figures to show that the thing is not quite so silly as it might at first appear. If you turn to page 49 of Stuart Chase's book, Government in Business, you will find, according to his figures, that the United States already had 51,000,000 of its total population receiving money from the government directly or indirectly right then. We are rapidly approaching that condition, so why should we not organize on a scientific basis so that -we can effectively give men purchasing power? How else are we going to get into their hands consuming purchasing power? The day will come when we shall look back at this time and wonder how we could have been so short-sighted as not to see that distribution of consumer credit was the solution for our problem. We should be taking measures to find out the exact conditions in our economic and national life and we should be preparing ourselves for the production of new money nationally created, nationally backed, so that it will be sound money, and nationally managed in the interests of all the people of the country.
We should be prepared to distribute purchasing power to the fullest possible extent by giving people work, yes, through reforestation, the building of roads, the erection of great public buildings and that kind of thing. But still the day will come when there will be vast numbers of our people who can never again be profitably employed and we must be prepared to give such people purchasing power through the direct issue of purchasing power. You may call it $25 per month, dividends, or anything else, but that must be done. These are the suggestions I offer. We should take forward looking measures and not
depend upon laissez faire and the hope that in some way we may grow out of this condition. I contend that we are suffering from a malady out of which we cannot grow.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin I should like to quote a few words of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). He said that extremes defeat their own purpose and that violent fluctuations one way or the other are mere leaps in the dark. I know there are many people who consider that the great province of Alberta, of which some Canadians are very proud, is making an experiment which is a mere leap in the dark. The Minister of Finance also said that he was not an alarmist, that on the contrary he was confident that common sense and sound economic policies could solve our immediate problems. We believe that the proper solution to our problems is different from the solution suggested by the orthodox economist, those to whom the previous speaker (Mr. Blackmore) referred to as laissez faire economists. I believe in the integrity, honesty and good judgment of the Minister of Finance and of this government, but the world has progressed and, as the previous speaker has said, we are living in a new age. New times demand new measures and new men.
When the Minister of Finance referred ta leaps in the dark which would be unwise to take, possibly he was thinking of untried experiments in finance. That is quite likely as he is the Minister of Finance. The greatest experiment being attempted to-day is the one being tried in Alberta. We wish to see that experiment succeed. We do not believe that all people are equal. I have heard it said by some in this house that giving dividends to all citizens would make them equal with each other; that to do so would be attempting to standardize humanity. We do not believe that all people are equal, neither do we believe that is is possible to give an equal opportunity to every individual. This cannot be done because of the fundamental difference in individuals in their capacities for taking pains, which is genius. We differ according to our genius and ability.
However we do believe in removing poverty and distress by giving dividends to everyone irrespective of whether they are poor or rich, We do not believe in making fish of one anc fowl of the other. According to biologists all living things furnish an infinite variety of form. If you observe the dandelion on the lawn or by the wayside you will see that no two are alike. People say that persons or things are alike as two peas in a pod, but we
The Budget-Mr. Hay hurst

know that no two peas in any pod are alike. There is a tremendous variety of form in all living things around us and we believe that all people are different. Because we believe this, we believe in removing the stigma of poverty or the dole from people so that they may be able to develop their own initiative and personal welfare, become real citizens of this great Dominion of Canada and contribute something to the greatness of our country.
Modern education realizes that all children are different, and we are proud of this. I have a family of my own and I know their individual differences. The natural capacities and attitudes of each individual should be developed to the full. That is the new education, and because it is the new education, we need a new economy and a new line of thought entirely different from the old. We believe that the payment of dividends will permit a greater choice of professions. Thus, the talent to be found in our young people will be given an opportunity to express itself. Poverty must be abolished so that the activities of mankind may have an opportunity to develop themselves in a more varied way than they have in the past.
The urge is to push back the frontiers. The mysteries of science and the wisdom of philosophers will ever challenge our mental capacities. We should try to abolish toil and drudgery. That is what science is for. Every little tool ever invented was invented in an effort to remove toil and drudgery so that our lives might be made more attractive. Life is made less sordid when our environment is cleaner, broader and happier. Initiative and competitive spirit will find an outlet in better production.
Social credit, which is not mentioned very often in this house, will not pave the way to a loafers' paradise, as so many people would have us believe. Some people hold the view that men will not work simply because they are receiving basic dividends, but labour will always be required to attend to the machines. Social credit will lead to more leisure, which in turn will bring about an increased production in necessities and luxuries. The social credit movement aims at economic security for every man and woman. Once the hazards of our physical maintenance are removed we shall be able to develop our individual differences unhampered. It has been stated by the members of the government, especially by the Minister of Finance, and by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), that a tremendous change took place in the financial world between October, 1929, and October, 1930. Is it reasonable to assume that the world was suddenly impoverished in those years? It is well known that for every loaf 
of bread which was baked we could have baked four. There was a surplus of practically every form of goods and there was also sufficient machinery idle to have increased the supply of goods threefold. The main trouble was that the purchasing power of the people had been largely destroyed.
The question is often asked: Where is the money to come from? Why should there be periods when there is a great insufficiency of money or purchasing power in the hands of the people, in these days when money is mostly paper in the form of cheques and bank notes? Money that is created by banks is usually called bank credit; it represents merely figures written in a book. There is no value in money of itself. Its proper function should be that of tickets to purchase goods, and the number of tickets to be created should be in precise ratio to the quantity of goods made for the people. The tickets would thus serve industry and the number would rise or fall in proportion to the amount of real wealth produced.
The first step in setting up the necessary machinery would be the establishment of a national credit account. We have heard nothing from the government about the establishment of a credit account, which is absolutely essential if we are to have, a new and better economic and social order. This account would give an estimate of all the nation's real wealth as represented by buildings, factories, railways and the capacity to produce. Money is the life-blood of industry and should be taken from the control of private individuals and handed back to the state, and the state should appoint experts to carry out the will of the people. Political democracy without economic security is a farce. The fact, which has long been obvious to a few and is now being recognized by many, is that the industrial nations are suffering poverty and insecurity in a world of enormous physical wealth simply because the incomes of individuals are too small to purchase goods. Modem power production with the wonderful machinery of to-day could supply the wants of everyone. Producers cannot now sell their goods because the incomes of the majority of people are not large enough. Incomes cannot under present conditions be issued fast enough to enable people to pay the prices asked for the goods produced.
The immediate need of the people to-day is a national dividend to enable them to purchase the plenty and security which money can buy. It has been proven conclusively, I think, by the previous speaker that an age

The Budget-Mr. Hayhurst
of potential plenty is at hand. Real wealth is possible immediately, but we are cheated out of our heritage, like Esau with his mess of pottage, by a faulty economic mechanism. Money in itself is worthless; it derives its value only from real things. If there were no real things for sale, things that people desire, money would be actually worthless. Does anyone deny that there is an abundance of real wealth, food, shelter, clothing and services, or at any rate that real wealth can be produced? The main purpose of production is to satisfy human needs as long as our productive powers permit. In this day of plenty the problem of production has been solved. Our financial system provides the means of distributing the things we produce; it regulates the distribution, collection and cancellation of money. The earliest distribution of goods was conducted on a barter basis; that is, goods and services were exchanged for goods and services. In time, however, we find a series of currency tokens. At first these tokens had an intrinsic value-cattle and gold, for instance-but such tokens eventually gave way to tokens without intrinsic value, which nevertheless can readily be exchanged for goods and services.
The trouble with the present financial system is that the ultimate control of money rests with the banks. In the Encyclopaedia Britanniea there appears this statement:
Banks lend by creating the means of payment.
This is a significant statement. They do not merely lend the means of payment but create it. Banks control the supply of cheque money and make it plentiful or scarce at their pleasure. Naturally moneylenders do not wish the people to be well off because they might cease to borrow; and what is worse, these financiers buy and sell money of other nations. They realize that people must have money and it is in their interest to keep it scarce. In times of inflation such as 1929 the banks were able to create nine or probably ten times as much new money as there was on deposit. The Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, in his book with reference to post-war banking policies, says that the amount of money in existence varies only with the action of the banks. This simply means that they are able to create credit at will, and as this credit performs the functions of money the bankers have the power of creating and destroying money at will. We are not opposed to bankers; they are men like ourselves. But we want them to carry out a policy which will be in the interests of mankind in general.
Credit should bear an accurate proportion to the amount of real wealth; but financial credit as we understand it, that is debt, does not do this. Credit which is provided by the modern financial institutions, and which is commonly called financial credit, is really debt credit. The monopoly of credit by the financiers should cease. These monopolists wish to keep the supply of credit and money scarce so that they may charge interest on it. Because the bankers control this money they are the real rulers. It is time the community took control; Canada should control its own credit. The credit of Canada, which needs no financing, may be called social credit. The attempt made by international financiers to gain control of the world by financial means, through the setting-up of international banker settlements, should be stopped. The Canadian people should be given their economic freedom and control of their own credit. Greater liberty and security would thus be given all the people. Canada could become overnight rich beyond the dreams of avarice. WTe have the potential capacity, the sources of supply; all we need is to control credit in the interests of all the people and not of a few.
It is evident that our difficulties lie not on the productive but on the financial side. Why do nations search for gold? I know in the budget speech it was said that this government will not propose discriminatory taxation with respect to mines. Of course we want all possible encouragement of enterprise in the development of mines. Under social credit gold because of its export value is just as valuable as under any. other government. The minister stated:
While the present government is in power, mining enterprises can depend upon treatment at least as favourable as that accorded to other industries under the corporation income tax.
It seems strange that nations should search for gold as they do, presumably because they believe gold gives more backing to currency expansion. Of course we know that even in Canada that is a fallacy. Periods of prosperity have always been coincident with new gold discoveries or produced by increasing the amount of currency relative to the amount of gold. Gold being a scarce metal has tended to make money tokens scarce. Currency manipulators who are interested in international finance and in the manipulation of currency and credits for their own selfish benefits are attempting to wreck a scientific age. Discoveries of gold have made nations rich, but surely the purchasing power of our people should not be subject to chance.
The Budget-Mr. Hayhurst

Gold or any other metal is a poor basis of money, because the value of money is governed by its quantity, and the quantity of paper money issued can be readily controlled according to the real wealth of the nation. Each nation should control its own credit and currency, and this should be issued in proportion to its production.
Possibly the greatest curse which has operated to control trade in the past has been the gold standard. It has been said that the gold standard is the basis of hatred; it begets war. It has been said that you might as well talk about a standard of love as talk about a standard of gold. It would really be better to call it a standard of hatred. It is a standard of scarcity, and because nations want to keep goods within the nations scarce, and export their surplus, very often they go to war with their neighbours to create markets. That has been the work of a few financiers' interested in the creation of debt in all countries. Upon no subject are the people as a whole so blissfully ignorant as upon that of finance, by which the wealth of moneylenders is increased at the public expense. Money should be controlled by the people of a state in the interest of all its citizens. Why give the control of the blood-stream of society to a few to use it for their own personal and selfish acquisition of power? The happiness of the citizens of any nation depends upon the policy of those in control of its credit, and that nation wherein the control is exercised for the good of the people will become the greatest nation in the world.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I wonder whether the hon. member would give us a short definition of just what he means by "credit control."

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is something
which is very subtle. For instance, we have the idea of a national government controlling a national bank. I do not know what the Liberal government proposes to do with regard to this national bank, but I understand they are going to bring forward a measure to buy fifty-one per cent of the shares. The bill has not yet come before the house, so I cannot speak with certainty, but fifty-one per cent of the shares would enable them to control the group of men who will sit at that caucus table, and through them, direct banking policy. We believe that the government should control the men who sit at that table. They should employ experts in finance who will control Canada's finances in the interests of the people. They should build up a national credit account, an account which will show all the imports, all the production of the nation, all the real wealth of Canada, and put

it down in a book, much as was done in the Domesday Book in England away back about 1080. The real wealth of the nation is shown on the credit side of the account, and we should constitute what we shall call a debit account on the other side. I may say that we did not hear anything in the budget speech about either a debit or a credit account. The debit account would record all the real destruction of property as it goes on to-day; it would show also our total exports. If at the end of the six months' period we had not more goods or a greater supply of real wealth than we had when we began, there would be something wrong with us as Canadians. We should have a greater capacity of production as the years go by and our credit power grows and develops. The balance would be the difference between real consumption and real production, and the surplus would be given to the people as a dividend, so that they could purchase the overplus, or the supply which to-day is destroyed.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member
one more question? If I understood him correctly, he stated that credit control must come through the Bank of Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I did not say it
came from the Bank of Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member built his
whole argument round it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am going to answer
t-he hon. member's question if possible. I say: If the people of Canada demand that the government of Canada control the policies of the banks, and if the people get behind the government, then they can control banking policy, because their representatives would not dare to oppose them. If the people of Canada demand a dividend they can get it, because they could elect enough people to see that that policy is carried out according to the real principles of the new economics. It is a unique opportunity for every person to get behind the movement for the emancipation of the people from the present money control. Orthodox economists call us heretics. Probably we are. In days gone by there were religious heretics; there were also political heretics; our fathers had to fight for political and religious liberty. But the greatest battle is still to be fought and won; it is the fight for economic liberty.
Think of who control the finance of Canada to-day. Have hon. members considered that wealth is more and more going into the hands of a few people? That being so, how can one expect to raise the standard of the people who are living in poverty and distress?

The Budget-Mr. Hayhurst
Dozens of them call at my home in the city of Ottawa, the capital city of this great dominion, asking for the bare necessities of life. There is plenty of wealth in Canada, but it is controlled by a few absolutely for their own welfare; they pocket the dividends. I am sorry that the Minister of Finance did not put a larger tax on some of the biggest incomes.
If each nation would control its own credit and its own monetary policy, it could be rich, in terms of real wealth, beyond the dreams of avarice. Skill in every human endeavour is wealth just as much as the farmers' wheat and the bakers' bread. The economic difficulties of the present time are largely due to the lack of the occupations for which many young men and women have spent time and money in training themselvesi. The previous speaker mentioned educational systems. Not long ago I read in the press that McGill university needed money in order to enable its young people to get a better education. There is the university; there are the professors; there are the young men and women, but they need money in order to provide an education. It is a tragedy that men and women at this stage of life should have their hopes shattered and their enthusiasms broken for lack of money. This would naturally lead us to the conclusion that there is something fundamentally wrong with society as it is constituted at the present time.
Possibly the subject least understood, because in past years it was considered a sacrilege to question it, is the subject of money, which controls our education, our life work, and which causes untold suffering through fear of insecurity, poverty and an old age unprovided for. Money is so vital to our welfare that the question of its control is the most important subject facing mankind to-day. Money may be said to exist in three forms, coin, notes and credit, of which a bank cheque is the most familiar example. Nine-tenths of all the world's money consist of credit of one kind or another. Control of our bank credit should be vested in the people, and the struggle for this control is the great problem with which the people of all modem nations are confronted. We have fought for our personal freedom. In the United States they had to fight in order to free the slaves. I suppose, sir, your ancestors were practically serfs; I know mine were. To-day, however, in the new age in which we are living, with the development of machines and so on, all that need not exist. In a degree we have obtained our political freedom, as hon. members know, through the reform acts of Great Britain as they have been applied to Canada. Our men and women have been given full
voting privileges, but to-day we must fight for our financial freedom. The great bankers of the world, practically without exception, have used expressions such as that used by Rothschild, who said, "Those who control the credit of a nation control in the hollow of their hands that nation's destiny." This subtle power which exercises control over parliament and industry, and which in turn is controlled by a feiw men for their own selfish interests rather than for those of humanity as a whole, must be brought within the control of the people of the nation.
We are now at the cross-roads of history. We have heard that expression before, but I believe it to be true. One road leads to untold prosperity through the organization of our power and technological improvements. The other leads back to the dark ages, which were the ages of scarcity, manual toil and human drudgery. The financial system as at present constituted must have booms and depressions. We talk about the boom of 1929 and the depression of 1932. We must have these booms and depressions in order that the financiers may retain control. It is the aim of the financial system to prevent good borrowers from accumulating money of their own, so when a boom has reached its peak those who have loaned money begin to call in their loans. Otherwise those borrowers would become too rich to want to borrow any more money. After a boom has progressed so far, high prices rule, and with high prices more and more money is required to carry on trade. Bankers have to honour their promises to pay, and as money is withdrawn from circulation the demand for goods decreases and goods fall in value, less money is loaned and a depression is started on its course. The banks follow the policy of alternate expansion and contraction of their loans and their purchases of securities. The business cycle which is caused by this policy brings in its wake bankruptcy, debt and the curtailment of industry. That is what we have passed through, a period of bankruptcy, debt and the curtailment of industry, through the curtailment of this purchasing power which should have been distributed more freely to all people.
The great prizes of this earth go to those who are in control of the financial machinery, bu't we believe that with human initiative and enterprise unchained it will be possible to have "a car in every garage and a chicken in every pot."

speechtext:
That sounds very nice to my hon. friends across the way. So many think that because we are financially poor, of necessity we must be really poor. We

The Budget-Mr. Hayhurst

know that money is not real wealth, but it becomes scarce and goods cannot be purchased. Money is one of the most ingenious and potent inventions of man, but people buy and sell money as a commodity, as other people buy and sell wheat. Real wealth decays, like the potatoes 'to which the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) referred this afternoon, but financial credit and debt have taken on the spirit of immortality. They are always growing; they always increase. We borrow the money with which to construct a building. The building deteriorates, but the debt increases. ^ I am reminded of those words of Goldsmith's:
111	fares the land, to hastening ills a prey,
Where wealth accumulates, and men decay.
Even in the days of Goldsmith they recognized the truth of the statement that finance controls the destiny of the people. The debts of countries and of individuals increase with each succeeding year. Thus we are establishing a debt creating structure whose subtle charm seems to hold the people in a hypnotic power. That is quite poetic for me. It is not suggested that credit should be so plentiful that unlimited quantities of money would be required to purchase the bare necessities of life. What financial expert would permit such a condition? At all times the credit supplied would bear a just proportion, neither too much nor too little, to the real wealth which a nation produced. It is like a man rowing in a boat on lake Superior. Would he jump overboard if he wanted a drink? Naturally we would not create huge amounts of credit, even though it only consists of figures in a book.
There are many monetary reformers today, as the house knows, but they are mere adventurers. When asked if they believe in dividends for all the people they immediately reply: No, we do not believe in people; we believe in the money system. They have no faith in their fellow men. Control and power mean more to them than the general uplift of all the people. How often has unemployment been held up as an incurable curse, when it should be looked upon as a triumph, and those unfortunate enough to be unemployed should have the satisfaction of knowing that they will always be paid. What a tragedy it is for those on the dole; there is the fear, the threat that to-morrow's dole may cease to be. Think of the tragedy of little children under the stigma of relief which has no permanency and which instils a fear of insecurity into their minds. I wonder whether any hon. members are living next door to families on relief. Will people be

able to unlearn the things they have learned and to alter the direction of their thinking before a greater crisis arises? Some people are afraid of a new crisis. We need not fear it, because a new crisis would take away the fear of poverty and insecurity. That nation, which I hope will be Canada, which produces real wealth in abundance should be the .greatest nation on earth, and will be the greatest nation if it gives purchasing power to its people.
Industry and all mankind are travelling in a vicious circle. Here is the question: Why cannot goods be sold? The answer is this: Because people have not the money. Why have not people the money? The answer is: Because wages are low; people are on short time, or are unemployed. Why are their wages so low? Why are they on short time or unemployed? Because factories cannot sell their products. Why cannot factories sell their products? Because the people have not the money to buy. No wonder poverty increases; no wonder bankruptcies and insanity increase. Perhaps there is no insanity in eastern Canada, but I am sure some hon. members think we in this comer of the house have a certain amount of it. I know, however, that in Alberta insanity is one of the greatest problems we have to face.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday afternoon hon. members listened to a most able presentation of the 1936-37 budget. Some of us who know the personal record and career of the gentleman who is now Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) could not help at least silently congratulating him upon the success of his career and the manner in which he carries the honours which have been heaped upon him. Concluding his speech the minister used this language, as reported at page 2391 of Hansard:
The government of Canada is making earnest and sustained efforts to meet this challenge and to grapple with the manifold problems of the country. I would ask the house and the

The Budget-Mr. Massey
country to accept the proposals I have made to-day as part of a conscientious effort to promote the best interests of the people of Canada.
Not for a moment would any hon. member question the sincerity of the minister, but perhaps some of us do not subscribe fully to the "efforts" or to the methods of "grappling." In the first place, not so many days ago, to be exact on Monday, April 6, we listened to the Minister of Finance use this language when speaking about the housing problem of Great Britain:
The great bulk of it has been, carried forward by the degree of confidence and leadership inherent in the people themselves, by the abolition of fear and the creation of confidence in the minds of men and women who have a little money, who need a home, to spend that little money in cooperation with the money of the state, possibly, in order to acquire that which they need. That is the sort of leadership we need in this country. We need confidence on the part of those who could do things by cooperation if only they did not fear so much.
Then, speaking on Friday when introducing the budget the minister said, as reported at page 2383 of Hansard:
That purpose the government intends to pursue steadily as an essential condition of the restoration of business confidence and the free functioning of private enterprise. This, it is believed, will contribute more effectively to the solution of the problems of unemployment and depression than any other single thing which governments can do.
I am not an alarmist. On the contrary, I am confident that common sense and sound economic policies can solve our immediate problems.
I wonder whether it tends to restore confidence to call the attention of the consumer, every time he makes a purchase, to the fact that his country is hard up and that he must be taxed accordingly.
Introducing the question of the sales tax the minister referred in his speech to the necessity for the tax. As I listened to him speak last Friday afternoon I could not help remembering "the forgotten consumer." My mind carried me back to the campaign of last year, during the course of which from one end of Canada to the other we heard presented the case of "the forgotten consumer." I am not standing in my place tonight to plead the case of the forgotten consumer or to draw attention to him or to her. Many people listened to what was said during the course of the campaign. If we may judge by the vote, many people felt that the forgotten consumer would be remembered.
I wonder whether it tends to create confidence in the present government when, in the first budget brought down after an elec-
12739- 162i
tion in which the forgotten consumer was proclaimed so loudly, we find an increase of 33J per cent in the sales tax. It seems to me that confidence must be shaken in the present government-and the minister has admitted that confidence is essential to recovery!
During the course of the last campaign many statements were made in an attempt to convince the electorate that the country faced a most serious situation. It was either "King or chaos," the insinuation being, of course, that chaos, if not already at hand, was just around the corner. On the air from coast to coast we heard language descriptive of that condition. There was a certain innocuous old gentleman who had a nasty mind, who was called "Mr. Sage," I believe. Mr. Sage had certain things to say, but they apparently did not mean very much, one way or the other. In one of the special committees we have spent a great deal of time in the last few weeks inquiring into who this innocuous but nasty-minded old gentleman was.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They ought to give Mr. Sage a gold watch and an illuminated address.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hazard the guess that
when prominent gentlemen, citizens of this country, take the air and proclaim from coast to coast that chaos is just around the corner far more serious harm is done than could possibly be done by an innocuous old gentleman with a nasty mind, who does not mean very much.
Confidence was shaken by many things that were said during the course of the last campaign. Confidence was shaken in the minds of many people, judging by the fact that they listened to the cry of "King or chaos." The first part of the speech introducing the budget should, I suggest, be spread from coast to coast and every Canadian should read it, for it is the written record of the results of the activities of the late government, and of which activities any government, Conservative or Liberal, might well be proud. This afternoon the right hon. leader of the opposition dealt fully with that fact.
In the second place, Mr. Speaker, and still along the lines of confidence, I would draw the attention of hon. members to page 2376 of Hansard where the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) used the following language on Friday last:
I direct attention to the fact that in the last fiscal year nearly 62 per cent of the dominion's revenues were required to meet fixed and uncontrollable expenditures, such as interest: war and old age pensions and superannuation; care of returned soldiers;
The Budget-Mr. Massey

subsidies to provinces and certain other outlay of this nature. In the year 1913-14, the last fiscal year prior to the war, only 19 per cent of the revenues were allotted to items generally regarded as uncontrollable, and even in 1929-30, when the effect of the war cost had been shown in our expenditures, the proportion was but 44 per cent, as compared with 62 per cent last year. Although it is not possible at this date, except by certain arbitrary assumptions, to make_ exact calculations, nevertheless it is obvious from an examination of the expenditure statements that the burden of the war cost, both direct and indirect, is even to-day a major factor in our budgetary situation.
We to-day as a nation, as part of a great empire, are definitely concerned in international affairs. We read the daily press with great care and much interest, and we realize that to-day once again over in Europe there overhang war clouds. The dispatches which we read are dated from London, Rome, Paris, Addis Ababa, or wherever it may be, but do we see a single dispatch on the war situation dated from Ottawa, Canada? Are we not a member of the League of Nations? Have not the people of this country a right to expect that those of us who are here representing them in this House of Commons should interest ourselves directly through the government in international affairs? War is preventable only when nations do not want war. Disarmament alone is not enough. Nations must be educated against war. There has grown up a generation since 1914-18 that knows not war, that had no experience with it. Figures such as I have quoted from the budget speech of last Friday are startling, and the minister says, "The burden of the war cost, both direct and indirect, is even to-day a major factor in our budgetary situation." His language should echo and reecho throughout this country to impress upon those who are young, and perhaps more foolhardy than those of us who are growing slightly older than we were, what the burden of war may mean.
There is in Canada a League of Nations' Society. Of its activities I have nothing to say. Unfortunately it is not a very prominent society. It is attempting to do its best in its own way, but does it receive support from this government? I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that confidence in Canada is the most important factor in her recovery, and one way in which Canada must demonstrate her confidence is to convince herself that in her own active field she is doing her bit to prevent war.
In the third place, Mr. Speaker, no one would question for a moment the desirability of balancing the budget. No one could question for a moment the desirability of taking
[Mr. Massey.l
steps in that direction. But what is the cost of balancing the budget? What is the cost of attempting to balance it to the degree suggested by the Minister of Finance? What confidence may be shaken in the process? Confidence! We have to-day in Canada a national radio. This is a medium that can be put to fullest use by this government for its own needs, not as a partisan government, but as the government of the nation, in an attempt to educate the people of this dominion that after all Canada has in the affairs of the nations of the world a position of which she may well be proud, and that, after all, we are not facing chaos but are, or at least were, on the road to recovery. Have we made any attempt to develop further any sort of newspaper or magazine campaign directed towards the restoration of confidence?
There also is the great question of the reestablishment of youth, on which on two occasions I have already spoken in this house. The other day some hon. member was speaking on pensions for those who voluntarily might retire from work at the age of sixty, and of what might be done in that regard. It was suggested by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean), I think, that it would cost 8522,000,000 to put such a plan into effect, a figure so astronomical that even the most powerful political telescope could not even locate it. Actually the cost of such a scheme might well be estimated at around $10,000,000, and what would such a scheme mean to the youth of Canada to-day as far as the opening up of jobs is concerned? What if the deficit is $100,000,000 or 8110,000,000 when the extra 810,000,000 might be put to such a service as that? To break the depression, means that confidence must be restored. I quoted from the words of the hon. Minister of Finance on April 6, referring to what the restoration of confidence had meant to the United Kingdom in connection with their housing program if in no other way.
In the fourth place I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether it builds confidence when industry commences to lose its position in its own home market. What does it mean when Canadian workmen lose their jobs or fail to get jobs as a result of the influx of foreign goods? How far-reaching is the effect? It might be said that there are only a few jobs lost, but what does that mean to a whole municipality, to a whole industrial centre? Five or eight hundred men out of work as a result of a change in the tariff may be a very small number as compared with the total number of men at work in

The Budget-Mr. Massey
Canada, but what is the effect so far as confidence is concerned? Who is going to be next? Those of us who live in industrial centres know full well the effect of the loss of a few jobs as a result of governmental action, and by a reduction of tariffs at a time such as this we are inviting the foreign manufacturer to sell in Canada, hoping, we are told, that perhaps we may be able to sell a little to him in return. Speaking on Friday last the hon. Minister of Finance, as reported at page 2368 of Hansard, said:
Imports from the United States for the full year just ended were $319,610,706, which is an increase of 16 million dollars over the preceding year. 7'2 million dollars of this increase were recorded in the first three months of this year under the operation of the trade agreement.
Over 56 per cent of our imports come from the United States. At the same time they take only 37 per cent of our exports.
One cannot listen to such figures as these without some degree of alarm. I have in my hand a report from the Department of National Revenue, showing the duty collected for the months of March, 1935 and March, 1936. In 1935 in that month, $8,395,859 was collected in duty while in the month of March of this year, $7,508,479 was collected. Thus in one year the loss of duty would be equal to one-half of the increase in sales tax revenue which the minister intends to collect if we may assume that that loss in duties is maintained for twelve months. In the face of such facts, do we contemplate further tariff reductions?
Let us take one class of goods only by way of illustration, the tariff on which is reduced by this budget. I refer to farm implements. I realize that in so doing I place myself in a peculiar position. My family's name has been closely identified with the implement industry in Canada for upwards of ninety years. Perhaps I may be accused of impropriety in introducing this subject and I do so at the hazard of being misunderstood. I should like to attempt to make my position as clear as I possibly can. I and my family have no connection whatsoever with the Massey-Harris Company, nor have I had for nearly four years. Some years ago I started to work in the shops of that company and until 1932 I was employed there. I left in 1932-I was not fired, I may say-to enter another sphere of activity. I worked in all the shops and ultimately became works manager of the Toronto factory
When I left, I left behind me in that factory a great many friends, men who had been pals of mine, men who earn their living with their hands, grand fellows in every way. As a member of parliament, I have an obligation to those men, not simply because they are friends of mine but because I know their problems.
When I speak of the men in the Massey-Harris factory I know whereof I speak. I have an obligation to them and I would be remiss if I did not raise my voice in this house on their behalf. It is on their behalf I speak. I am not much interested in the implement industry as an industry, but I am deeply interested in the men employed in the industry and in their jobs. I am a protectionist. When I say "protectionist" I do not refer to the protection of industry; I refer to the protection of jobs. That is the way I interpret protection, and that is why I am a protectionist.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what protection is.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It seems to me that the way in which we can increase our home market most effectively is by paying wages to men. The reduction of the duty on farm implements to 7J per cent does one thing and one thing only; it spells disaster to the implement industry of Canada. This means that the jobs of 18,000 men are threatened by the introduction of this tariff.
Let me refer to one particular company, the Massey-Harris Company. In the last ten years that company has paid in wages and salaries, $37,312,000; it has paid in commissions to agents, $10,817,000; in pensions, $1,020,000, a total of $49,149,000. That is not a bad contribution to the pay-rolls of Canada. Has there been exploitation of the farmer during the course of this business?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sure.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Those who do not know say, "sure." This company has experienced a loss, from 1930 to 1935, of $25,700,000. Does that	look like	exploitation?	Then in thetwenty years from 1916 to 1935 there has been a net loss of $7,400,000. Many weeks ago we listened to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) reading a long list of implement prices, showing changes from 1913 down to the present day. Do hon. members know that since 1913 wages have doubled, western freight rates have increased 38 per cent and eastern freight rates, 83 per cent, and that there have been	many changes in design	due to thedemands of the farmers themselves. For instance, there has been developed a one-way disc seeder which performs simultaneously the four operations of ploughing, harvesting, seeding and drag-harrowing. This machine sells at a	saving of	$286 to the	farmer eventhough its selling price is $420.50, or the cost of four machines needed to perform the four	operations	it performs	would total
$706.50. The operating costs of those four machines would be $1.40 per acre, whereas the operating cost of the one-way disc seeder is 47 cents per acre.
The Budget-Mr. Massey

The Canadian implement companies have been challenged in connection with Canadian as against American prices. It is interesting to compare American and Canadian prices in a list of thirteen major machines, including an eight foot binder, a twenty double-disc drill, a five foot mower, et cetera. Taking the prices at Oswego, Montana, and Consul, Saskatchewan, the Saskatchewan prices are only 94-54 per cent of the Montana prices. Taking prices at Sweet Grass, Montana, and Coutts, Alberta, the Canadian prices are 98-96 per cent of the Montana prices. Taking Pembina, North Dakota, and Emerson, Manitoba, the Canadian prices are 99-73 per cent of the American prices.
Will a reduction in the duties mean a saving to the farmer? That is the question. Let us see what has happened. In 1935 the total volume of implement business in the United States was valued at $360,000,000, whereas the total volume of the Canadian implement industry in the same year was valued at only $16,000,000. In 1935 one company in the United States had a turn-over in that one year greater than the turn-over of all Canadian companies in nine years. Take the years from 1926 to 1935, in some of which the duty was low. There were $139,000,000 worth of implements produced and sold in Canada as against $165,000,000 worth of implements imported into Canada. How long can an industry expect to continue with that sort of set-up?
Why should I, with no interest in the industry as an industry, stand here and attempt to plead its case? Why should I or any other member rise in this house to plead the case of this industry? Was there not a committee set up to investigate this whole matter, to give the implement industry of Canada a chance to present its own case before anything was done? Was there not a committee set up to see if the farmer were being damaged and if the implement industry were playing the game? I believe that committee is still sitting. There were handed out to the implement industry questionnaires which would require some three months to answer at a cost of many thousands of dollars, many of these dollars having been spent already, but has the industry yet been permitted the opportunity to plead its case? Why should I or any other member stand and plead the cause of the implement industry when there is a tariff board before which that industry might have appeared? For the reason that the case has been prejudiced! The alleged criminal has been apprehended and sentenced before trial. That is not British, Mr. Speaker.

I am sent here by an industrial riding; I am sent here to represent the industrial worker, and so long as there is breath in my body and red blood in my veins I will plead his cause. And I say to-day that the jobs of 18,000 men are at stake. Yes, and how many more jobs are there at stake in industries which contribute raw materials? Sympathize with the farmer? Of course I do. I know something of his problem for I have been privileged to stay on farms and I know many farmers. Of course I sympathize with his problems. This country owes him a debt of gratitude which it can never repay. But will this tariff benefit him? That is the question. And will the government juggle with the jobs of 18,000 men hoping that perhaps it may benefit the farmer? And to what end? Why pick on one industry? Let us consider other commodities which the farmer buys. Tlhe price per pound of implements is 12-80 Cents in Canada. The prices per pound of a number of articles the farmer uses are as follows:
