Why not inquire into those industries having protection running up to 35 per cent and down as low as 15 per cent, whose products are listed above, and whose prices are more per pound than those of the implement manufacturers? Out of every $100 the farmer spends, he spends only $3 on farm implements. There was an increase in the prices of farm implements on January 1, 1936, of 3J per cent which means, to the farmer, ten cents out of every $100 he qpends; and yet there was a shout to high heaven that made the welkin ring with the hideousness of the cry.
One must admit and admit readily, that prices of commodities purchased by the farmer, implements included, are definitely out of joint with the prices of the things

The Budget*-Mr. Woodsworth
he produces. But is it reasonable to expect to estimate the price of a binder in accordance with the price of a bushel of wheat and have that relationship always hold true? Yes, and why take just one industry? Among all the industries that sell goods to the farmer, why single out one and expect that a slight difference in price will readjust the whole situation for the farmer?
I have said what I have said only because I am a member of parliament representing an industrial riding and it is my pledged duty to do all in my power to protect the jobs of the people who elected me.
I am at a loss to understand the attitude of some hon. members who cry free trade in farm implements and make that cry without lack of knowledge of what they are saying when they advance the mouldy doctrine of free trade. Surely the creation and preservation of the home market is dependent upon the payment of wages. Let us assume-and this figure is the best one I could possibly obtain-that the average family food bill in Canada is $400 a year. This means that the annual family food bill of the families dependent upon the implement industry is $7,200,000 a year! Let us assume that the price of implements is reduced by the full 17i per cent of the duty that has been taken off since the first of January of this year. That would mean to the farmer 52J cents out of every S100 he spends. And for this are we prepared to jeopardize a market, his market, to the extent of $7,200,000? Is that reason?
In conclusion, and in words similar to those of the Minister of Finance, let it be assumed and hoped that the government of Canada is making an earnest and sustained effort to grapple with the manifold problems of the country. Confidence-it has been the keynote of what I have attempted to say to-night. Confidence-it is a great word. Confidence- it is the prime prerequisite to complete national recovery. Confidence-let every step taken by this government be a step towards restoring confidence.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I must congratulate the
Minister of Finance upon his very clear and comprehensive statement. I welcome the downward revisions in the tariff; that it seems to me is all to the good, notwithstanding the position taken by the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Massey).
A recent writer pointed out that the ancient Romans built roads and the Chinese built walls. The Romans went forth to conquer the world while Chinese civilization became very largely stagnant. I believe there is a little parable there for us all. We cannot
very well live behind walls; we must build roads to the wider society about us. But I venture to say that in these days we need to build not merely physical roads and we need to do more than lower tariff barriers; we need to build roads along new lines instead of trying to conserve old institutions and to hide behind them. Instead of doing that we should strike out along new lines. The alternative is build roads or build walls.
The minister admitted that agriculture was very far from being in a satisfactory condition, but he did not suggest any means by which we could materially help that industry. I was reminded of the statement of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) a few days ago to the effect that it was useless to repair the superstructure of our economic life as represented by our secondary industries if its foundation, as represented by our primary industry, is crumbling away. I regret that although he made that statement, he actually advocated back-to-the-land policies, and certain members talked of a better balance between the cities and the country. I would urge upon the house that it is largely useless for us to try to bolster up the secondary industries, as we have been doing in the past, and as we are continuing to dio, if we allow our primary industries to languish. It is all very well to point out with pride that we have moved up from the eighth to the sixth place among the nations in total world trade. That does not help very much unless the majority of the people of this country are living a satisfactory life. I was surprised that in his excellent speech the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), although he was able to quote quite extensively concerning the financial condition of the agricultural industry and the prices of farm implements, and although he was pleading for the workers in industry, had nothing to say with regard to the real wages paid. I should have liked to have him give at some length the wages paid to all grades of labour in the agricultural implement industry.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
permit an interruption? The average for 1935 was 45 cents an hour for all classes of work.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does that include salaries?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That includes hourly wages. Putting in salaries would make it too high; the hon. member might question it.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I should like to ask the hon. member for Greenwood where he gets these figures of the average wage in the implement industry.
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Possibly it is a
little out of order for the discussion to go on, although I too would like to secure the source of these figures, and also the sources of some other figures used by the hon. member for Greenwood. I should like to know where he got the figures as to what proportion of a farmer's income was used in the purchasing of farm implements.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Anybody can get those who wishes to work out the statistics.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, possibly. I would point out, coming back to agricultural matters, that Canadian farmers were in the happiest condition before we developed industry in this country at all. At that time they lived a self-contained life. Instead of industry helping the farmers to a fuller and richer life, it has in fact impoverished the farm life of this dominion. I think we must recognize that.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I for one do not want to go back to the past. I do not think you can turn the clock back. But I do say that a readjustment is necessary, and that in that readjustment the farmer must not be neglected as he has been in the past.
The minister tells us that industrially and commercially conditions are beginning to show improvement. He pointed out that an analysis of the record of earnings of 241 leading Canadian corporations discloses that net earnings are about eight per cent greater for the fiscal year than for the previous fiscal period. That statement in itself might be satisfactory, but let me put two others alongside of it. The second statement he made was that common factory labour was up 2-4 per cent. I was not quite clear whether that meant that the total wage bill was up 2-4 per cent or that individual wages went up 2-4 per cent. But in any case I do think it is very unsatisfactory. We find a rise of eight per cent in industrial improvement, that is for the industry itself, and only a 2-4 per cent rise in the wage bill. The minister seems not to have taken those two into consideration and placed them side by side, or he would hardly have gone on to increase the sales tax from six per cent to eight per cent, because that tax falls most heavily upon the poorest of our people. It may be said that the corporation tax was increased. That is true. But the corporation tax is very largely passed on, as the minister knows. The minister shakes his head. I am sure he must have read the financial statements of the great corporations where they 
definitely arrange for the corporation tax before even declaring their dividends.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, but, if my hon. friend will permit me, the corporation tax is definitely a tax on earnings. I agree with him that most taxes are passed on, but this is a tax which is not payable unless the earnings are made. That is, it is definitely payable out of earnings.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But it does not come out of the individual; it comes from the general public. My point is that the individual's tax is not readily passed on, whereas essentially the corporation tax is passed on to the general public.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In the next year's budget. It does not rest on the individual as an individual income tax does. The sales tax also is a burden on every individual consumer. It seems to me that if the minister had put those two statements of his together and looked at them carefully-the one statement that industrial and commercial earnings are up eight per cent-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
"An analysis of the record of earnings of 241 leading Canadian corporations discloses that net earnings are about eight per cent greater for the fiscal year than for the previous fiscal period." Those were the exact words that the minister used. I say that if they are up eight per cent and factory labour is up only slightly over two per cent, we might have expected that the taxation on the industries would have been greater and that on individuals would have been lessened, instead of having the sales tax increased as it is.
The minister declares that dominion credit must be protected at all costs. In that, he represents the attitude of big business. I am one of those who challenge the attitude of big business in that regard. In a general way I recognize that our interests are all interrelated, but I do not think it follows that because big business is prosperous the great majority of the people are necessarily prosperous.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Neither do I.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad of that. But the credit of the country, we are told, must be maintained at all costs. That means in effect that in several western provinces we have to cut down on the costs of relief, of education, and of social services of all kinds. "Credit must be maintained at all costs!" A few weeks ago the minister said he was quite

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
sympathetic with the idea that there should be pensions to the blind, but under present conditions he could not find the money. The credit of the country must be maintained at all costs! Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that the credit of the country so-called can be maintained at all too great a cost to the mass of the Canadian people. The minister makes that argument the basis for the proposed loan council legislation. Personally I think some such legislation as that is almost an inevitable development. But I submit that it is a dangerous thing to centralize financial control unless at the same time we centralize responsibility for social services. If we are going to take the position that the dominion government should take care of our education, our hospitals, our unemployed, our old people, then a good deal might be said for some such arrangement as a loan council. But if it means, as I think it must mean, that financial men will be very largely in control and that they will assume the attitude which the minister has enunciated, that is that the dominion credit must be maintained at all costs, then I say that the situation ahead is very serious indeed.
The minister made another statement which is half true and half false, when he said that foreign trade was the very lifeblood of Canada. Well, it is consoling to know that we are to have an increase in the dressed and dyed rabbit skins that come to us from Belgium. I do not know whether that is an indication of how vital trade is to this country, but I should like to quote a statement by the dominion statistician under date of December 20, 1932. The proportions are not much different to-day, I should think.
It would appear that in 1930-
This was at the last census, I assume.
-the net value of production (i.e. value of products less the cost of any raw materials involved), amounted to $3,216,747,000 in value, whereas our exports amounted to $885,996,000.
The difference was consumed in the country.
The minister exalts something like one-quarter of our entire production to the predominant position. I do not think that is a fair way to look at the situation in Canada. Foreign trade, says the minister, is the very lifeblood of Canada. Well, it should be remembered that it is only a quarter of the entire production which is given that exalted position. If we swept foreign trade aside altogether, we would still consume in this country three-quarters of the entire production. I quite agree with the hon. member for Greenwood when he urges that we should develop the home market. We should do that; we should pay wages to everyone, and see that the wages are as high as possible.
That would be the surest way of taking up the apparent overproduction that we have in certain Canadian industries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who would be here to pay the wages?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We would all be here to pay the wages. As to foreign trade I quite recognize that certain commodities can be produced to greater advantage in other countries than in Canada, and we should have a certain amount of what really should constitute trade, the exchange of the things that we could produce to advantage for the things that could be produced to advantage elsewhere, but I urge that it is not the profit motive which should lie behind an exchange of that kind. As I have said before in this chamber, I believe that the old basis of foreign trade, which is the shipping of our production in order to make profit, will have to be altered, and that the foreign trade of the future will have to be on the basis that I have just indicated.
Again, the minister says that in the fiscal year just ended our gold sold abroad amounted to $119,000,000. I like the phrase, "our gold," but I should like to ask the minister who owns most of the gold mines in this country. If I am rightly informed a considerable amount of the stock of those gold mines is owned abroad. It should be "our" gold, but it is not "our" gold. The dividends about which the minister thinks so much are paid not so much to the people of this country as to foreign investors. Who owns the gold mines? It is true that the miners get wages, sometimes very pitiable wages too, but in the gold mines they are always in danger of that dread disease silicosis, which is carrying off so many of them. We hear very little about that. Oh, no, it is not "our" disease; we do not boast of that, nor do we boast of "our" wages that are paid to the gold miners, but it is "our" gold! Again, there is in this connection something into which I have never inquired very carefully, but I should like to ask the minister to explain at some time just what are the arrangements with regard to depletion allowances. It has always seemed to me that, if we are going to make depletion allowances, one of these days, especially with the very high percentage that is allowed, depletion will theoretically be complete. My idea would be that if these mines have been alienated from the crown, and if allowances are made for depletion, once the depletion is complete the mines should revert to the crown. Why not?
Then there was a statement made by the minister which I was very glad to hear, that there was a payment of $272,000 to maintain reserves in the government annuities fund.

The Budget

Mr. Woodsworth
In this connection perhaps I should call attention to a mischievous article which appeared in Saturday Night of April 25 of this year, entitled Life Insurance versus Social Security, by some writer named Mr. W. A. McKague. I quote one statement from that article:
The dominion government has some $23,000,000 of deposits in its post office savings bank, and some $40,000,000 belonging to those who have paid for annuities. Where is this money now ? ... what we find is that there are no real assets-the money turned in by depositors and by purchasers of annuities, has been all drawn into the bottomless pit of expenditure, and has gone the way of other receipts from taxation and borrowing.
Is that true, Mr. Minister? If it is not true I think we should have a statement from the Minister of Finance. It does not seem fair that we should allow such propaganda, condemnatory of governmental institutions and containing so many misleading statements as are contained in the article to which I have referred, as well as some other articles in the same issue.

speechtext: Did I understand my hon. friend to ask me a direct question?

speechtext: Yes, and some time I should like to have the minister answer it.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am very glad to hear that statement from the minister; I wanted to get that. Would the minister mind explaining just how this payment of $272,000 to maintain the reserve in the government annuities fund is handled?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

It is part of the consolidated revenue fund. From its very inception payments made by annuitants have gone into the consolidated revenue fund. The contracts represented by the annuities are a charge on that fund, which is the money of

Canada. The money owned by the people of Canada is charged with the annuities. That is about the simplest way I can express it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
I do not wish to
have the time for the minister's explanation taken off the time allotted to me to speak, but possibly he could explain briefly how the payment of $272,000 to maintain the reserve in the dominion annuities fund is handled.

speechtext:
It is a payment made
to bring the reserve up to the actuarial requirements stated to exist for the fund. It is to keep up the basis. The expectancy of life in the meantime has increased, tending to lower insurance rates but to raise annuity rates. My hon. friend follows me?

speechtext:

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I also recall
that the minister stated that the interest burden last year was $134,550,000, or an amount which used up 36-2 per cent of our total revenue. I should like to emphasize what a heavy burden that is.
We have heard a good deal about old age pensions, but in this year old age pensions use up only 4-51 per cent of the total revenue. Therefore, heavy though the charge

The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth
may be, It is veTy small when compared with what we pay to those who hold the bonds of Canada. Then, although we have heard a great deal about unemployment relief, and the terrifically heavy burden it has placed upon us, we find that relief expenditures last year were only $51,987,307, including expenditures on public works and in the drought area. Hon. members say that is an enormous sum? Yes, but it is not much more than a third of the burden entailed by interest charges.
The minister has said that we must do something to make an appreciable approach to balancing our budget. He desires to have a definite and positive program which will assure the attainment of our financial objective within a limited period. Is it not possible that the government now only entering office might have something like a five year plan, under which we could look ahead not for one year but for five years? I was interested to note that Mr. Thomas Bradshaw, president of the North American Life Insurance Company, made the following statement at the general meeting held on January 20:
Whatever we may think of Soviet Russia's five-year plan, or that set forth in the recently issued book. The Next Five Years, and to which - general support was given by a group of 152 of Britain's outstanding men and women, representative of all shades of thought, there is much to be said for the intelligent planning of the future over a definite term of years, and adhering as closely as possible to program.
It seems to me that notwithstanding the uncertainty of the future something of that kind is much better than what might be called the hand-to-mouth policy prevailing to-day. We plan only a few months ahead. I do not like to be too severe in my criticism of the government at this time, because it seems to me that it is facing a task of trying to work a system that is rapidly becoming bankrupt.
To-day the leader of the opposition referred to the sales tax as a possible indication of the approaching end of the capitalist system. There are many other indications. The large number of people on relief that cannot be absorbed into employment is a good indication that the system cannot be maintained much longer. It is true that the minister is making some little effort to balance the budget. He is not nearly balancing it this year, and I cannot see that he has given any ground for hoping that he can balance it next year. When we have reached the point where we can balance our budget only by increased borrowing, thus pyramiding our debts, it seems to me that this is another
indication that something is radically wrong with the system.
The minister points out that there are two main obstacles to balancing the budget, the cost of unemployment relief, amounting to $51,987,307 and the deficit of the Canadian National Railways amounting to $42,590,000. The sum of $5,818,000 has to be added for the eastern lines, making a total of about $100,000,000. Let me point out that in this connection the minister did not mention the large amount of $134,000,000 for interest charges. That is, in singling out these great obstacles one might also have thought the Montreal Star was talking.

Oh, no; that is the

Yes; as some of these bonds have matured they have been
The Budget-Mr. Woodsworth

renewed at a lower rate of interest, but the amounts are not relatively very great, and we are not doing anything on a large scale to bring down this enormous burden of interest charges. That is the point I want to emphasize. Further than that, the budget might be balanced in another way, and that is by increased revenue. I would point out to the minister that the income tax amounts to only $66,808,000. Is not that correct?

Indeed, why not go a little further than income tax and make a levy on wealth? We have very large sums of money concentrated in a few hands. Why should there not be a levy on wealth in order to lessen the burden of the debt? They are doing it in other countries in one way or another. They have an inheritance tax in Great Britain, but there is nothing of that kind in Canada so far as the federal government is concerned. speechtext:
I have before me the correct figure on the income tax. I said in the budget speech:
The increase in tax revenue is more than fully accounted for by the income tax which yielded $82,700,000 as compared with $66,808,000 in 1934-35.
My hon. friend took the figure for 1934-35, and did not allow for the very large increase which took place in income tax revenue in the last fiscal year.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was quoting the figure for the yeaT before from the minister's own statement of revenues.
With regard to income tax, two considerations stand out sharply in an examination of1 the income tax returns for Canada: (1) The folly from a financial point of view of taxing small incomes, and (2) the wide range remaining for higher taxes on the higher incomes. An analysis of the 1934 returns yields the following:	93,316 taxpayers with incomes
under $2,000 paid $989,083; 6,133 taxpayers with incomes of $10,000 to $50,000 paid $12,199,435; and 307 taxpayers with incomes of over $50,000 paid $8,785,854. The income classes are defined as "taxable incomes." The minimum exemption in 1934 was $1,000. Consequently the "net income" for this group ran as high as $3,000. Therefore the revenue of $989,083 comprises the total derived from all taxpayers whose income was not more than $2,999. I would submit that in taxing small incomes the Minister of Finance is evidently not influenced by financial considerations. He could get far more revenue by taxing a little more heavily the people of greater wealth.
The real measure of the severity of income taxes is the income which is left to the taxpayer after his tax is paid. The person of small income pays his full share of the cost of government quite apart from income taxes. The head of a family with a small income pays heavily in customs taxes and in sales tax. The amount of these taxes paid by the wealthy head of a family is not a great deal more than that paid by a person of small income. Certainly the greater amount paid by the man of wealth does not increase proportionately to his wealth, very far from it. An analysis of the tax revenues of the dominion in 1934 shows that the most profitable source of revenue for the Finance minister, from the financial point of view, is the group of classes whose taxable income ranges from $10,000 to $50,000. An analysis of this group yields the following results, and Mr. Speaker, with the permission of the house, I should like to place this table on Hansard:

None of these taxpayers would be poor if his tax were doubled, and most of these taxes would stand trebling. Take, for instance, the man with an income of from $25,000 to $30,000. The minimum income he had left after the tax had been paid was $20,875. So he would be very far from poor. It follows, of course, that there is also abundant room for increasing the taxes above $50,000. The materials for detailed analysis are, however, not available. In fact, the former Minister of Finance told the house that the information was not in the public interest.
In closing, may I point out that while the minister is apparently trying to preserve a very conservative point of view with regard to public financing, the situation is very rapidly changing the world over, making changes in policy highly imperative. I might quote the concluding paragraph of an interesting pamphlet, the Formation of Capital, issued by the Brookings Institute:
At the present stage in the economic evolution of the United States, the problem of balance between consumption and saving is thus essentially different from what it was in earlier times. Instead of a scarcity of funds for the needs of business enterprise, there tend to be an excessive supply of available investment money which is productive not of new capital goods but of financial maladjustments. The primary need at this stage in our economic history is a larger flow of funds
through consumptive channels rather than more abundant savings.
I cannot see why taxation should not be definitely and consciously used for an adjustment of the wide discrepancies which now exist in the distribution of wealth in this country. The Minister of Finance the other day had this to say:
There must always be a limit to the extent to which money can be taken from all of our citizens of Canada to be given to some of our citizens of Canada.
He had in mind that there must be a limit to social services such as unemployment relief which, in his opinion, took from all-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I must inform the hon. member that his time has expired.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will just finish my sentence, Mr. Speaker. As I understand the Minister of Finance, he says that there must be a limit to these social services which involve the gathering from all to give to some, but may I point out to him that to a considerable extent his budget is taking from all of us to give to a very small group of the people of Canada. This government is becoming a vast debt collecting agency through which we turn over the greater portion of our revenues to a small group of bondholders and other people who to-day are largely the recipients of those amounts now classed as "uncontrollable expenditures," which constitute some sixty-two per cent of the entire revenues of this country.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would hardly be correct for me to say that I am disappointed in the budget. Realizing, as I d'o, that the Liberal party is a reactionary party, I do not look for any
The Budget-Mr. Quelch

really progressive action which would lead us to permanent prosperity. I do not believe there is any solution within.the narrow confines of the present capitalist system. It is true that rates of interest on the new dominion loans have been reduced, but as the national diebt is only a fraction of the total bonded debt of Canada and as these low rates are not being extended to the provinces and municipalities, it is hardly to be expected that the bonded debt of Canada will decrease. At no time during the last twenty-three years, even in times of the greatest prosperity, has Canada proceeded without going progressively further into debt. So long as we continue to operate under a debt-creating system, so long shall we be bound to go further into debt.
Many of those who voted in the last elections were of the belief that the government of Canada would issue its own credit, but from the statements of various Liberals, it has become very clear that such is not the policy of the government and that it intends to still go on pledging the real wealth of Canada to the financial interests. Such action can be continued only by keeping the standards of living down to an unnecessarily low point. We shall find that the present intolerable situation will be made even worse by the placing of an eight per cent sales tax on the consumer which will undoubtedly tend further to reduce his purchasing power.
The main problem to-day is that of stimulating the purchasing power of the people to a point where it is equal to the capacity of industry to produce and deliver goods. Any necessary increase in taxation should be made against surplus incomes, that is, incomes sufficiently large that the recipients are under the necessity of spending only a portion as purchasing power.
Some people take the stand that the government has no right to issue credit against the real wealth of the nation held collectively, when it is actually owned individually. We are actually doing that to-day in the form of dominion bonds. Bonds are nothing more or less than promises to pay at a future date. These bonds are recognized as a sound basis for the issue of money, for the issue of legal tender. Legal tender is recognized by the banks as a sound basis for the issue of credit up to nine or more times the amount of money held by them. That being the case, and as the federal government issues the bonds, why cannot the government issue credit backed by legal tender, with the full resources of the nation behind it?
I believe this example has been given before, but I should like to give it again just to

bring out my point. In November, 1932, the federal government sold to the chartered banks of Canada $35,000,000 of treasury notes bearing interest at four per cent. The banks increased the government deposit by $35,000,000. Then, in a short time the banks applied to the treasury board for a currency loan of $35,000,000, under the provisions of the Finance Act. The government issued the new currency and charged the banks three per cent, the security put up by the banks being dominion government notes. Why could not the government have credited themselves with
835,000,000 of currency in the first place and thereby saved the nation many millions of dollars annually? This is pointed out by Sir Thomas White in the November, 1935, issue of the Canadian Bank of Commerce Review, which states:
When credits are created in favour of customers, whether borrowers or savings depositors, a bank must be always prepared to meet cash demands of depositors-in legal tender. This is the reason why a bank must always keep liquid to the extent found necessary under the experience of bankers in the conduct of the business along safe lines. To maintain the requisite degree of liquidity, varying with varying conditions, banks must hold a considerable percentage of the assets (about ten per cent of their liabilities) in legal tender.
When 'the banks received the loan of $35,000,000 in currency they were then in position to loan out from $300,000,000 to $350,000,000 at interest. The currency loan itself was based upon treasury notes, which in turn were based upon the real wealth of the nation. We claim that the nation could have issued that credit in the first place, thereby saving the people of Canada millions of dollars in interest. I know many people would call this inflation. For instance, the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deach-man) is reported on page 1854 of Hansard as follows:
When you give something to the unemployed you in reality give them a call upon goods; and when you do that by printing money I do not think you will get very far, because your money will not be of much value and you will find it a great deal more difficult to finance than you did before. When you borrow money what do you do? You take from people who have and give them in return a certain allowance called interest; we pay them for the use of their money with a promise, which I hope we shall make good, of repaying them in due course when the time comes. But when you print money what do you do? You start upon a course of inflation-
I am sure the hon. member for Huron North would not have u>s take that statement too literally. He said, "When you borrow money you take from the people who

The Budget-Mr. Quelch
have," and yet Sir Thomas White says, "The banks can loan up to about ten times the amount of their cash deposits." The Macmillan report states on page 34:
It is not unnatural to think of the deposits of a bank as being created by the public through their deposits of cash, representing either savings or amounts which are not for the time being required to meet expenditure. But the bulk of the deposits arise out of the action of the banks themselves, for by granting loans, allowing money to be drawn on an overdraft, or purchasing securities, a bank creates a credit in the books which is the equivalent of a deposit.
I quote from a speech delivered by the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, in January, 1925, as follows:
I am afraid the ordinary citizen will not like to be told that the banks can create or destroy money. We do not like to hear that some private institution can create it at pleasure. It conjures up a picture of an autocratic and irresponsible body which by some black art of its own contriving can increase or diminish wealth and presumably make a great deal of profit in the process.
We find, therefore, according to these financial experts that when we borrow money from the banks instead of borrowing money already in existence, we are borrowing newly created money, and the total deposits of the banks are written up by that amount. The point is that it is new money. Therefore, if under certain conditions when we borrow money from banks it is inflation, so also under the same conditions if we borrow money from the government it will also be inflation. On the other hand, if under certain conditions the oreation of credit by banks does not cause inflation, then the creation of credit by the government under the same conditions cannot cause inflation. So long as only sufficient credit is issued to balance effective purchasing power with the total collective volume of prices of goods available for distribution, instead of having inflation you have stabilization. This is upheld very well by charts of Mr. Carl Snyder, chief statistician of the New York Federal Reserve Bank. These charts were published in the May, 1931, issue of the Royal Bank of Canada Economic Review, and Doctor Donal Marvin, Royal Bank economist, commenting on them, says, in part:
This relationship between volume of production and trade and volume of credit is one of the most important discoveries which has ever been made bv the statistician. It implies that there is a mathematical relationship between the volume of production and credit on the one hand and the price level on the other. In fact, by dividing each volume of credit by the corresponding volume of production, the level of prices at any particular moment is approximated.... Can it be that
had the growth of credit paralleled the increase in the volume of production and trade, there would have been no substantial changes in the general price level, no major business cycles, no booms, no severe depressions? This is indeed a startling concept, affording hope that the social injustices inherent in all major changes in the general price level might be avoided by proper control of credit.
It would seem therefore, according to Doctor Donal Marvin, that so long as you do not issue more credit than the volume of production and trade, there is no real danger of inflation. Nevertheless I realize that it would be a dangerous procedure to endeavour to equate the volume of effective purchasing power with the volume of potential production of ultimate goods unless first of all effective means were introduced to control prices so as to establish a fair price level based upon cost of production. The actual level would not be so important as would be the bringing about of a fair relationship between wages and prices and ensuring that the price of one article was commensurate with the price of another. Then, once having established a fair relationship, the purchasing power of the people could be raised until it was equal to the total collective volume of prices of ultimate goods, by an issue of credit direct to the consumer. This payment would have to be made outside the present industrial system because as credit passes through the industrial system it accumulates costs in excess of the purchasing power it distributes, thereby failing to bring about an equation as between purchasing power and prices of ultimate goods.
Whilst advocating a change in ownership of the banks, I realize that this in itself would be useless unless the policy of the banks were also changed, because owing to the policy of the banking system at the present time the volume of financial credit in circulation at any given time bears no relationship to the requirements of the people. It is argued that the restriction of credit is forced upon a banking system by their knowledge of conditions. This claim, however, is not upheld by some notable authorities on banking. Mr. W. L. Baker, former superintendent of branches for the Standard Bank of Canada, in a criticism of the system and not as a monetary reformer, referring to the great deflation of midsummer, 1921, states:
The reduction of $43,000,000 in three months was not a national slacking-off of industry, but was without doubt due to the concerted action of the banks in curtailing and calling in loans in all directions, and contributory in a general way to other conditions which were calculated to stagnate industry.
So we may believe from this statement that instead of loans being called in on account of
The Budget-Mr. Quelch

a general falling off of business, it is just the contrary,, that business falls off on account of restriction of credit by the banks, resulting in the closing down of factories and increased unemployment. This action is to a certain extent no doubt forced upon the banks on account of their practice of loaning promises to pay up to ten times the amount of their actual cash, with the result that in times of great expansion they become panicky as soon as their margin of safety has been reached.
To quote again from Mr. Baker:
Bankers easily take fright. As demands for loans increase, in direct ratio comes their unwillingness to lend. When result of curtailment comes in decreased business activity, they raise the cry, "Now is no time to borrow; we are calling in our loans; you must restrict operations." And the cycle of deflation sets in, hastened by an ever-increasing timidity of bankers.
As an example of such panic I would refer the house to a statement made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) in a speech at Toronto in November, 1933. He is reported as having stated that from September, 1929, to September, 1933, $932,000,000 was taken out of circulation. No one would suggest that that was a natural slacking off of industry.
Money is termed a measure of value, but we find it at present to be a very elastic measure, at times swelling and at times shrinking, and we have placed the power of expanding and shrinking the dollar in the hands of a private monopoly so that they can manipulate this measure to their own advantage. When they expand credit at a greater rate than production the dollar shrinks, and when they restrict credit so that it fails to keep parallel with production the dollar expands, bringing about in a general way a depression with its consequent misery and bankruptcy. At such times we find the credit houses taking over these bankrupt concerns at a fraction of their real value., and later on selling in a time of expansion at a considerable profit to themselves. Such cases I have known in the west. Such power should not be placed in the hands of any private corporation, because their large profits can be made only by the general exploitation of the public.
Then, again, we are told that the banks are anxious to loan money to-day but that they cannot find reliable concerns willing to, borrow. Industry is not prepared to expand until it is assured of a market for its products, and as industry fails to distribute sufficient effective purchasing power to -buy back its own production, consumption has to be financed by direct relief or a program of capital goods

production. This condition applies not only to Canada but to a majority of nations, with the result that every nation is endeavouring to sell more goods than it buys. But, if we take the world as a collection of nations endeavouring to sell more than they buy, the absurdity of the situation becomes apparent, resulting in international friction.
We in this comer take the stand that the main justification for foreign trade is to export our surplus production and exchange it for those commodities which we cannot produce economically in Canada. The chief point to remember is that if there is an insufficiency of purchasing power available to buy the total production of the country, there will also be an insufficiency of purchasing power available to buy the goods for which our surplus products are exchanged. Therefore we contend that the main problem confronting this government is to stimulate the puchasing power of the people until it is equal to the capacity of industry to produce and deliver goods. In the past we have endeavoured to accomplish this by production credit, and we have failed in our objective, for the three following reasons: Every creation of credit has been at the same time the creation of a new debt. By the very nature of its existence it has been interest bearing. Lastly, as this new credit passes through the present industrial system it will create as many additional costs as it subsequently cancels, thereby failing to bring about an equation between consumption and production. We therefore claim that in the future we must recognize the absolute necessity for financing consumption by consumption credits. This credit money might well be .paid in the form of a dividend directly to the consumer so as to ensure as high a standard of living for our citizens as our total productive capacity might be able to supply.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I desire to make a few remarks during this debate. I wish to say something about unemployment and sound money, because I believe those are the keys to our trouble.
In bringing down the budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) stated that while trade had largely recovered, employment had not kept pace with production. That is true also in the United States. We have been told that the vital things to-day are to balance the budget and to put everybody to work. But I suggest that the vital thing to-day is to abolish poverty and destitution, and that the way to do this is neither to balance the budget nor to put everybody to work, because I believe that it is quite impossible designedly

The Budget-Mr. Jaques
to do either, let alone both. We cannot tax ourselves into prosperity, and we cannot borrow ourselves out of debt.
It is claimed that England has balanced her budget. But that is a result, not a cause. It is the result of spending vast sums of money on munitions and housing and other national programs, and her budget has been balanced only by going further into debt, while there are still two millions unemployed and half her population is undernourished. An individual may balance his budget by saving, but a nation can balance its budget only by spending more money.
Worth while employment and really sound finance are the results of sound economic conditions, which are the maximum production of goods and services, and that is absolutely dependent upon maximum consumption-the exact opposite of tightened belts. The latter policy, which is called sound money, is really unsound. For sound money is scarce money, and scarce money means underconsumption, and therefore underproduction and unemployment. What we can and ought to do is so to adapt our financial system that we can produce to the limits of our powers and consume to the limits of our desires. We can do no more, and we should do no less.
I have heard in this house a great deal in favour of hardship and poverty, and that these twO' conditions are necessary for the morale of the people. If this is true, then unless members of the House of Commons are supermen many of us are in deadly peril from working under very pleasant conditions and being by no means badly paid. Evidently this does not worry a number of the members. It does not worry the advocates of sackcloth and ashes; but then, of course, they are supermen. My belief is that we are no better and no worse than the people who send us here, and if it is right and proper that we should work under these pleasant conditions and should not be-as we certainly are not-destitute, then I say it is right and proper that those who send us here should work under the most pleasant conditions possible and be as far removed from destitution as this country can possibly afford.
I agree with the Dean of Canterbury when he says:
It is a poor estimate of mankind that would hesitate to cure its ills for fear of its misuse of health.
He says, also:
Poverty is a dangerous disease. It breeds sickness and evil manners, and in our efforts to avoid it wre feed the very fires which produce the ruthless and acquisitive man.
Neither of those types is altogether desirable as a citizen; still less are they desirable as legislators.
It is proposed to encourage or to force people back on the land to do subsistence farming. This seems to meet with favour in this house, especially from those who know nothing about it and who have no intention of learning. The test is simple: Would you desire it for your wives and children? Well, I know what it means, because I have lived it. I say it is not good enough for my wife and children, and therefore it is not good enough for the wives and children of those people who sent us here. Absolutely, it is not good enough. I believe that true Christianity, sound economics and common sense are inseparable. If it can be shown-and it can be -that subsistence farming or any other unnecessary work or hardship, for that matter, is not common sense, then I submit that it will neither help to balance the budget nor preserve our morals. It will do the very opposite. In the main these people are unemployed because they have been replaced by machinery, and if the products of the machines are to be distributed those who have been displaced must be provided with enough purchasing power to buy back those products, or the machines must stop. Farming to-day is highly mechanized, yet it is proposed to turn thousands and perhaps hundreds of thousands of people into the bush armed with axes and picks and shovels, to make a living practically with their bare hands. I have seen the results. These people have no purchasing power; they cannot even buy tea, sugar or coffee, still less radios, decent linen and the other commonplaces of modem production. They cannot even send their children to school, because they have not the clothes with which to send more than one child at a time. Of what possible use are such people to the industrialist? Subsistence farming is not common sense to-day. There is much to be said for the simple life, but the simple life is not a sordid struggle for a mere existence; it is not a philosophy of "root hog or die," and it is quite impossible without economic freedom.
No man can serve two masters. No man can serve sound money and the people of this or any other country. What of the majority of those who are working in industry? Sweated wages cannot buy back the products of sweated industry. That is common sense. But if scarcity cannot be induced in the home then tyranny cannot be imposed in the factory. That also is common sense as well as true Christianity. We social crediters say that the object of industry is neither work nor wages but the production and distribution of goods

and services, and1 the only sound economy is that which will produce and distribute the maximum amount of goods and services with the minimum amount of work and trouble. That is pure common sense. Further, we claim that under the existing financial set-up it is impossible to distribute enough purchasing power to sell what is produced; that is a mathematical truth. The orthodox economists deny it, but they are paid to twist the facts to fit theories, whereas we try to fit theories to the facts, and that also is common sense.
Let us for a moment consider the replacement of men by machines. I remember some years ago working in a jam factory. It was a cooperative affair, and the local berry growers used the factory as much for the purpose of obtaining work and wages as they did for making jam, so that no effort was made to instal machinery. While that lasted, of course,
it was all right,	but after a	time other	companies came in	who wanted	to make	jam,pure and simple. Well, they installed all the machinery they could and employed as little labour as possible; consequently they were able to undercut the prices of this cooperative factory. The cooperative company got into difficulty; the	government	foreclosed	themortgage and they went out of business. Two or three years ago I was through that factory again, and the superintendent showed me all this automatic	machinery.	Where I	had
pushed and shoved there were belts, conveyers and every modern convenience. I congratulated the superintendent upon his ingenuity and he said, "Yes, it is all very fine as a factory, but what I would like you to tell me is this: If we do not pay out the wages who is going to eat the jam?" If anyone can answer that question I should be very glad to hear it, because outside social credit I do not think there is an answer to it. It may be said, of course, that machinery as used in those factories will cause work of other kinds. I happen to know the history of many of those people who worked with me in that factory, and I can assure hon. members that to-day if they get their bread they certainly are not getting any jam on it.
What is the remedy? We believe that we must finance consumption so that what is produced can be distributed. Let us look after consumption and production will look after itself. We propose national dividends. We consider Canada to be one great going concern and its citizens to be shareholders, and as such entitled to dividends. No one is better qualified to speak on this subject than that very great Englishman, Doctor Hewlett Johnson, scholar, scientist, engineer and Dean of Canterbury.
